items.summary: The 10 May 2024 geomagnetic storm, referred to as the Gannon Storm in this paper, was one of the most extreme to have occurred in over 20 years. In the era of smartphones and social media, millions of people from all around the world were alerted to the possibility of exceptional auroral displays. Hence, many people not only witnessed but also photographed the aurora during this event. These citizen science observations, although not from scientific instruments operated by observatories or research groups, can prove invaluable in obtaining data to characterise this extraordinary event. In particular, many observers saw and photographed the aurora at mid-latitudes, where ground-based instruments targeting auroral studies are sparse or absent. We created an online survey and circulated it within networks of aurora photographers to collect observations of the aurora and disruptions in technological systems that were experienced during this superstorm. We obtained 696 citizen science reports from over 30 countries, containing information such as the time and location of aurora sightings, observed colours and auroral forms during the geomagnetic storm. We supplemented the obtained dataset with 186 auroral observations logged in the Skywarden catalogue by citizen scientists. The main findings enabled by the data collected through these reports are that the aurora was widely seen from locations at geomagnetic latitudes ranging between 30° and 60°, with a few reports from even lower latitudes. This was significantly further equatorward than predicted by auroral oval models. The reported auroral emission colours, predominantly red and pink and intense enough to reach naked-eye visibility, suggest that the auroral electron precipitation contained large fluxes of low-energy (< 1 keV) particles. (...)

items.title: Impact of Structural Design on Magneto-Mechanical Resonators: The Case of a Jewel Bearing Variant
items.summary: Magneto-mechanical resonators (MMRs) are passive, wirelessly read sensors whose small size, miniaturizability, and low cost make them attractive for tracking and for sensing physical and chemical quantities. Their operation relies on a permanent-magnet rotor whose mechanical resonance encodes the sensing and tracking information. The bearing suspending this rotor is therefore decisive both for in-operation performance and for manufacturability. The original design suspends the rotor on a thin thread, which is nontrivial to assemble. This work investigates the impact of that structural design choice by introducing an alternative bearing in which the spherical rotor magnet rests in a cup-shaped industrial jewel. A dynamic model of this Jewel-MMR is derived, including the angle-dependent dry friction torque at the jewel contact. From it, a geometric trade-off between friction torque and resilience against unwanted oscillation modes is identified. Since the conventional quality factor loses its meaning under dominant dry friction, a two-tiered framework is proposed that compares MMR variants by estimation precision at equal magnet size and natural frequency. Both variants are characterized at a fixed pose on a Helmholtz-coil detection platform. The Jewel-MMR is self-aligning, requires fewer adhesive bonds and alignment steps, and the prototypes built here were assembled in less than half the time. Its response signal decays faster, so that under laboratory noise conditions the natural frequency and the orientation are recovered more precisely from the thread variant; these orientation figures quantify repeatability, not absolute accuracy. The jewel bearing, however, tolerates larger deflection angles and thus a stronger signal, which reverses this relation above a noise level determined in a simulation-based robustness analysis, indicating an advantage at reduced signal-to-noise ratio.

items.title: A heuristic sketch how it could fit all together with time
items.summary: On a scientific meta-level, it is discussed how an overall understanding of the physical universe can be built on the basis of well-proven theories, observations, and recent experiments. In the light of almost a century of struggle to make (common) sense of Quantum Mechanics and to reconcile it with General Relativity, it is proposed to (for some time) forget about quantizing gravity or striving for one Theory of Everything or 'Weltformel', which would describe the whole of reality seamlessly without any joints or suture marks. Instead of one single monolithic formalism, a three-legged compound approach is argued for. Quantum Mechanics, Relativity and Thermodynamics are proposed as the main pillars of reality, each with its well-defined realm, specific features, and clearly marked interfaces between the three of them. Not only classical reality, which is rather directly accessible to us, is then comprehensively modelled by their encompassing combination. Quantum phenomena are understood as undoubtedly lying at the bottom of classical physics and at the same time, they become 'fully real' only when embedded in classical frames, i.e., preparation and measurements in time. It is then where thermodynamics steps in and provides the mediating glue as it does at interfaces towards gravity. Decoherence is understood as a smooth way of gradually transferring information and basically dumping entropy to a suitable environment. The aim of this short contribution is not to deliver novel quantitative results but rather to propose a comprehensive research program and to coarsely lay out a very roughly coherent sketch starting from the beginning of the one universe, which we inhabit. The all-embracing picture is claimed to be one of ('mutually induced') emergence.

items.title: Maximum likelihood, neural networks and posterior mean for inferring fractional Brownian motion parameters
items.summary: Fractional Brownian motion (fBM) is a model of anomalous diffusion parameterised by a Hurst exponent $H \in (0,1)$ and a generalised diffusion coefficient $D_H > 0$. We jointly estimate $H$ and $D_H$ using maximum likelihood (MLE) from density measurements with Poisson counting noise and single-particle trajectory with Gaussian localisation error. We show that one density measurement in time cannot infer both $H$ and $D_H$ and that several time points are needed, which matters most for inference precision. For trajectories, we show that a neural network trained with a squared error loss approximates the posterior mean of $H$, which can be computed exactly at negligible cost. Paired with the profile-likelihood estimate of $D_H$, the posterior mean has the lowest root mean squared error in both $H$ and $D_H$, except near $H=0$ and $H=1$ where MLE estimates $H$ better. In vesicle trajectories from two cell types, $H$ and $D_H$ form a continuum rather than distinct modes of motion. The posterior probability that each window within a track is subdiffusive or superdiffusive shows that $26\%$ of MRC5 fibroblast and $21\%$ of HeLa vesicle trajectories contain both subdiffusive and superdiffusive windows, against $2\%$ and $7\%$ expected from estimation uncertainty alone. Intracellular cargoes therefore switch between subdiffusion and superdiffusion over time rather than forming populations with fixed $H$.

items.title: Generative modelling for multivariate spatio-temporal downscaling of monthly climate fields
items.summary: Inferring climate fields at higher spatio-temporal resolutions from coarse representations is essential for accessing socioeconomic and environmental impacts. The downscaling of modelled climate fields faces a trade-off between data storage constraints, simulation efficiency, and resolution requirements. While many methods for spatial downscaling have been proposed, joint spatio-temporal downscaling has received comparable little attention. When deriving, for example, daily fields from climate datasets that are available only as monthly averages at coarser spatial resolution, it is highly challenging to faithfully reproduce extreme event statistics and spatiotemporal consistency. To address this task, we introduce a generative machine learning approach, using a diffusion model to jointly downscale monthly temperature and precipitation fields into temporally consistent daily fields at higher spatial resolution. We demonstrate that our approach can generate high-dimensional multivariate climate fields at daily temporal and 0.25° spatial resolution from monthly input fields at 1° spatial resolution, exhibiting coherent temporal dynamics and physically plausible spatial structures. In particular, by incorporating a conditional guidance technique, we show that a pre-trained diffusion model can be directly leveraged to efficiently generate daily high-resolution fields conditioned on monthly inputs, without requiring additional fine-tuning or retraining. Our probabilistic approach thus provides an efficient and generalizable framework for spatio-temporal climate downscaling, enabling flexible climate fields generation for climate impact assessments and digital Earth simulator constructions.

items.title: Tracking large chemical reaction networks and rare events by neural networks
items.summary: Chemical reaction networks are widely used to model stochastic dynamics in biophysical processes. Their exact probabilistic description via the chemical master equation becomes intractable for high-dimensional systems due to the exponential growth of the state space. This difficulty is further exacerbated when metastable transitions and rare events dominate the dynamics. Here, we present an advanced neural-network approach that effectively tackles large reaction networks and rare-event dynamics within a unified framework. Building on autoregressive representations of the full joint probability distribution, we achieve efficient training through second-order optimization methods, including natural gradient descent and the time-dependent variational principle. We leverage enhanced-sampling strategies that enable accurate resolution of low-probability regions governing rare transitions. We demonstrate the method on a multistable genetic toggle switch and a mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) cascade consisting of 16 species and 35 reactions with dense coupling. We further quantify rare events in spatially extended Schlögl models in both one- and two-dimensional lattices, reaching system sizes with extremely large state spaces up to $3\times10^{15}$. These results highlight the potential of neural modeling as a flexible and scalable framework for studying high-dimensional chemical reaction networks and rare events.

items.title: Topological photonics in nanoscaled systems with far field radiation and polarization singularities
items.summary: Topology is a powerful framework for controlling and manipulating light, minimizing detrimental perturbations on the photonic properties. Combining nanophotonics with topological concepts presents opportunities for both fundamental physics and technological applications. Although most topological photonic realizations have been inspired by condensed-matter analogue models, new topological ideas have just begun to be realized at the nanoscale. Nanophotonics is characterized by subtle phenomena that are not usually considered in other topological models' realizations, such as nonlocality, strong field confinement, and light radiating to the far-field continuum. In this perspective, we will discuss how standard topological band theory for photonic crystals needs to be extended by a more comprehensive approach that properly treats such nanophotonic intrinsic effects and, in particular, the interplay of polarization and far-field radiation. We highlight the emerging role that polarization singularities might play in defining the topological invariants in the far field, which are not fully captured by bulk observables alone. We conclude by outlining a set of open questions and promising directions for exploring novel concepts in topological nanophotonics and shaping next-generation photonic devices.

items.title: Magnetic field induced modulation of heat transport in CrPS$_4$ probed by TaIrTe$_4$ transverse Seebeck thermometry
items.summary: Understanding and controlling heat flow in low-dimensional magnetic materials is central to thermoelectrics and spin caloritronics. One of the challenges is the absence of sensitive probes of small, field-dependent modulations in thermal transport. Here we demonstrate transverse Seebeck thermometry using exfoliated TaIrTe$_4$ as a probe of thermal conductivity modulated by an external magnetic field on a van der Waals magnet, CrPS$_4$. With a temperature gradient oriented at $45^\circ$ to its principal crystallographic axes, TaIrTe$_4$ exhibits a transverse thermopower exceeding $200~\mathrm{μV\,K^{-1}}$ for 900 nm wide and 30 $μ$m long electrodes, enabling precise detection of variations in the local temperature gradients. Exploiting this with CrPS$_4$ in a nonlocal geometry, we resolve distinct field dependent thermal conductivity changes associated with both the spin-flip and spin-flop magnetic transitions which we attribute to variations in the magnon$-$phonon coupling in CrPS$_4$. At 5 K, the transverse Seebeck response is modulated by more than 8$\%$ by an external magnetic field, demonstrating strong magnetic control of heat transport in CrPS$_4$. This all van der Waals platform offers high sensitivity to modulations of thermal conductivity and a broad adaptability to a wide range of exfoliated magnetic systems.

items.title: Online reduced-order modeling from primal solver trajectories for PDE-constrained optimization
items.summary: Repeated high-fidelity state and gradient evaluations make large-scale PDE-constrained optimization computationally expensive. Reduced-order modeling provides a natural way to reduce the cost of these repeated high-dimensional computations. However, existing reduced-order modeling approaches often rely on converged high-fidelity states for model construction or updating, while their reduced spaces may lose accuracy as the design moves beyond the region represented by the available data. To address these limitations, we present Reduced-order Trajectory-based Optimization (RETO), an online framework that constructs local reduced-order models (ROMs) directly from unconverged primal solver trajectories. Each local ROM is built from snapshots collected during a finite number of high-fidelity primal iterations, without requiring full-order convergence, and supports multiple low-cost state evaluations, adjoint-based gradient evaluations, and design updates. New solver trajectories are generated at updated design points to reconstruct the local ROM and continue the optimization. Across three distinct PDE-constrained optimization problems, RETO achieves solution quality comparable to that of full-order optimization, with speedups of approximately 8 to 22 times in cases without discontinuities in the state fields. Even in the transonic inverse-design case involving moving shocks, RETO retains an approximately threefold speedup. The transonic results further show that the online local ROM progressively captures evolving shock-related flow features as new primal solver trajectories are incorporated. These results demonstrate the value of unconverged primal solver trajectories as an online information source for reduced-order optimization, allowing the reduced basis to evolve with the design rather than requiring a basis that covers the entire design space in advance.

items.title: Pauli-type coupling between spinors and curved spacetime
items.summary: We investigate Pauli-type interactions generated by minimal coupling of a specified covariantly regular representative of the Dirac Lagrangian. A derivative-quadratic term proportional to a length parameter $\ell$ is a total divergence in free flat spacetime and leaves the free Dirac equation unchanged. After electromagnetic coupling, it is equivalent, up to a divergence, to a Pauli operator with coefficient $-q\ell/6$. We explain how a specified comparison between measured and predicted anomalous magnetic moments constrains this coefficient, separating historical illustrative scales from a conditional statistical bound. In metric-compatible Riemann--Cartan spacetime, the same construction generates torsion-dependent derivative couplings and a spin-curvature coupling. In the torsion-free limit, the latter reduces to the scalar mass coefficient $m+\ell R/12$. On prescribed pure-axial and pure-vector torsion backgrounds, the characteristic form admits superluminal wavefronts relative to the spacetime metric in its nonzero-torsion Lorentzian regime; sufficiently large spacelike effective torsion instead leads to degeneracy and an ultrahyperbolic characteristic form. For the observed cosmological constant and illustrative microscopic values of $\ell$, the vacuum mass correction is negligible. High-curvature applications and the characteristic structure of the full coupled theory require a specified gravitational action and further dynamical analysis.

items.title: Density and excess molar enthalpy of 2-butanol + glyme liquid mixtures. Application of the DISQUAC, UNIFAC (Dortmund) and ERAS models to 2-alkanol + linear ether systems
items.summary: Densities and excess molar volumes ($V_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$) at (293.15 to 303.15) K and excess molar enthalpies ($H_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$) at 298.15 K are reported for the 2-butanol + 2,5-dioxahexane, or + 2,5,8-trioxanonane, or + 2,5,8,11-tetraoxadodecane, or + 2,5,8,11,14-pentaoxapentadecane systems at 95 kPa. Densities were measured using a densitometer Anton Paar DSA 5000, and excess enthalpies by means of a micro-calorimeter Tian-Calvet. $H_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ and $V_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ data are positive, indicating that interactions between like molecules are dominant and that the main contribution to $V_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ is the interactional one. Our enthalpic data together with data from the literature have been used to evaluate the enthalpy of alcohol-glyme interactions, which are ranged between ($-$31 and $-$22) kJ mol$^{-1}$. From the comparison with $H_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ results for glyme + heptane systems, and from the position of the investigated mixtures in the diagram $G_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ (excess molar Gibbs energy) vs. $H_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$, it is shown that interactions are of dispersive type. 2-Alkanol + dipropyl ether (DPE), or + glyme systems have also been studied using the DISQUAC, UNIFAC (Dortmund) and ERAS models. According to ERAS results, physical interactions in glyme systems are dominant, while association effects are predominant in mixtures with DPE. The DISQUAC interaction parameters suggest that interactions related to the OH/O contacts are essentially dispersive. UNIFAC fails when representing thermodynamic properties of the studied solutions.

items.title: The BRUIT-FM "open data" noise reduction challenge
items.summary: The BRUIT-FM Challenge asks participants to reduce ''noise'' --- defined as any signal that masks the signal of interest --- on an open dataset of real and synthetic broadband seafloor seismology data. The dataset includes signals from earthquakes, ocean infragravity waves and seafloor currents. It also includes training datasets of synthetic data with reference solutions. Participants are asked to remove or separate these signals to obtain the best earthquake and seafloor compliance signals. The authors will make a first assessment of the submissions, based on noise reduction, signal deformation and ease of use. Participants are invited to a community workshop, in which they will validate the preliminary assessment and collaborate on a community paper describing the results, identifying promising pathways and proposing new directions. The best results will be added to a new version of the dataset, which will persist as a benchmark for future developments.

items.title: Assessing the effect of error field penetration during plasma current ramp-up in the DIII-D tokamak
items.summary: This work provides evidence that established error field penetration threshold scalings remain applicable during plasma current ramp-up. In dedicated DIII-D experiments with imposed $n=1$ perturbations during extended $I_p$ ramps, an apparent empirical threshold is found between $2$ and $3$~kA of applied 3D coil current, above which MHD modes are seeded. The imposed perturbation couples to the rational surfaces present during the ramp, seeding near the $q=4$ surface and penetrating as an $m/n=3/1$ mode by the end of the perturbation phase. To interpret these observations, multi-machine penetration threshold scalings are combined with equilibrium-based overlap metrics from the GPEC code, including the in-situ error fields of the device. This modeling reproduces the observed onset in the amplitude scan and classifies mode seeding across a database of 12 ramp-up discharges spanning a range of plasma currents and densities. Across this database, the seeding appears to be controlled primarily by the applied 3D coil current rather than by the plasma current or its ramp rate. Accounting for the in-situ error fields is found to be important for reliable prediction. These results are consistent with the robustness of scaling-based penetration metrics when coupled to detailed 3D field modeling under transient ramp-up conditions, and suggest the importance of accounting for in-situ error fields when assessing additional externally induced perturbations. This work is motivated by future tokamaks in which transient, non-axisymmetric error fields can arise during startup, for example from runaway electron mitigation coils.

items.title: Computational compressive imaging reconstruction with a simulated-annealing-based Ising solver
items.summary: Computational compressive imaging, such as single-pixel imaging and lensless imaging, is a promising imaging technique, enabling the reconstruction of objects from under-sampled measurements through compressed sensing algorithms or deep learning methods. However, the demand for electronic computational resources grows rapidly when recovering high-resolution and multi-dimensional images and training neural networks with numerous parameters, which has become a bottleneck for the widespread adoption of this technique. Here, we propose a physics-driven reconstruction framework that formulates imaging inverse problems as Ising models and directly recovers target objects through the self-evolution of non-von Neumann Ising machines toward the ground state of the Hamiltonian. We employ a simulated-annealing-based Ising solver to demonstrate this proof-of-concept by reconstructing objects in both single-pixel imaging and a lensless diffuser camera at sampling rates ranging from 1% to 25%. By further incorporating a foreground-sparsity constraint and a smoothness constraint, the reconstruction quality of our method is comparable to or even better than that of mainstream algorithms. This approach has the potential to substantially reduce the electronic computational burden of inverse reconstruction, paving the way for real-time, low-power computational imaging.

items.title: Unmasking Compensating Errors in Numerical Weather Models: A Process-Additive Neural Network Approach
items.summary: This work introduces a Process Additive Neural Network (PANN) framework to disentangle compensating biases in atmospheric models, where errors in different physical processes can offset each other and obscure their origins. Using a single-column model, each PANN branch represents the tendency error associated with a separate physical process, and the summed branch outputs approximate the total error relative to a reference tendency. Once trained successfully, the branch outputs are expected to provide process-level error attributions and, when averaged, estimates of process-level bias. Initial experiments focus on cloud-related processes in OpenIFS SCM case studies, where cloud and convection tendencies are strongly coupled and compensation is difficult to diagnose using standard approaches. The aim is not to replace human interpretation of physical processes, but to extend it to regimes where model complexity, process interaction, and compensating errors make direct diagnosis difficult. By providing a physically structured form of machine-learning interpretability, PANN can help connect complex model behaviour with process-level explanations. This work supports both improved understanding of compensating errors and the development of more physically consistent weather and climate models.

items.title: Quantum-enhanced phase interrogation of a fiber-optic strain sensor
items.summary: Fiber-optic sensors enable high-sensitivity measurements of various physical parameters. Here, we demonstrate a quantum-enhanced interrogation of an all-fiber-optic Fabry-Perot resonator, employing entangled two-photon interference to probe directly strain-induced optical phase shifts. The resonator is interrogated by a narrow-linewidth laser that is frequency-locked to its resonance mode, thereby exploiting the cavity's inherent sensitivity to variations in the fiber length. To access the phase fluctuations transferred to the interrogation field due to external perturbations on the sensor, we implement an in-fiber Mach-Zehnder interferometer readout. This configuration allows the sensor to operate both with classical coherent light and with entangled photon pairs generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion. Harnessing two-photon entangled states corresponding to an N = 2 NOON state, we experimentally demonstrate a reduction of the measurement noise below the standard quantum limit. These results provide clear evidence of the quantum advantage in enhancing fiber-optic sensors under practical constraints on optical power.

items.title: 1/f frequency-noise reduction in nanomechanical resonators by dissipation dilution
items.summary: The frequency noise of a resonant nanomechanical sensor is well understood down to its thermomechanical limit, but the longest useful averaging time is set by a flicker, or $1/f$, frequency-noise floor whose origin has remained unknown. We show that this floor is the thermal noise of the tension. By the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, the tension of a resonator with fixed ends fluctuates by an amount set by the loss angle of its material; for structural damping, these fluctuations produce $1/f$ frequency noise with a flicker coefficient $h_{-1}=E k_{\mathrm{B}} T/(2πVσ_0^2 Q_{\mathrm{el}})$, with $Q_{\mathrm{el}}$ the intrinsic loss under elongation, that contains no free parameter and is diluted by the tensile stress $σ_0$ in the same way as damping is in dissipation dilution. Silicon nitride strings and membranes from 30 to 340~nm thickness follow the predicted volume scaling, the predicted $σ_0^{-2}$ dilution across resonators and within stress-engineered strings, and the predicted thickness dependence, which places noise-active two-level systems in the volume and at the surfaces of the resonators, all at the absolute level set by the independently measured intrinsic loss. The same relation accounts for published data between 78 and 296~K; below 78~K, the loss measured at the resonance no longer represents the loss probed by the noise, marking the limit of the structural-damping assumption. Dissipation dilution therefore lowers the $1/f$ floor, and the longest useful integration time of a resonant sensor is set by its prestress, volume, temperature, and intrinsic loss angle.

items.title: Social Norm Diffusion in Societies: Simple or Complex?
items.summary: Social norms are a fundamental component of society, shaping how we communicate, cooperate, and avoid conflict. Despite their ubiquitous presence and profound influence on behaviour, questions remain about how they spread from person to person and whether they are adopted. Using an evolutionary game-theoretic model, we study whether simple or complex contagion processes characterise how social norms spread. Crucially, contagion type is endogenous and emerges from the model. We also vary cultural conformism, the cost of following a norm, and network topology to assess the generality of our results. We show that social norms in our model can spread through simple contagion when a new norm is low in cost and cultural conformism is low, while norms spread through complex contagion when the new norm is costly and cultural conformism is high.

items.title: Generalized Noether theorem in the realm of Hamiltonian point dynamics
items.summary: Noether's theorem in the realm of point dynamics establishes the correlation of a constant of motion of a Hamilton-Lagrange system with a particular symmetry transformation of its action functional. Although usually derived in the Lagrangian formalism, the Hamiltonian formalism provides a natural context for this correlation. Canonical transformations preserve the canonical form of the action up to a boundary term. Within the class considered here, a symmetry additionally preserves the functional form of the specified extended Hamiltonian. Every smooth phase-space first integral admits locally a corresponding canonical Noether symmetry when momentum-dependent transformations and boundary terms are allowed. In order to represent symmetry mappings that include a transformation of time, we use the extended Hamiltonian formalism. This formalism enables us to define generating functions of canonical transformations that also map time and energy in addition to the conventional mappings of canonical space and momentum variables. The physical energy hypersurface and the choice of the evolution parameter are distinguished from identities on the full extended phase space. As an example, a manifest representation of the symmetry transformation associated with the Runge-Lenz invariant of the Kepler system is derived. A suitable choice of evolution parameter makes its time-shifting representative a symmetry of the specified extended action.

items.title: Physics at the Edge: Benchmarking Quantisation Techniques and the Edge TPU for Neutrino Interaction Recognition
items.summary: This work presents a benchmark of quantisation techniques for convolutional neural networks applied to neutrino interaction recognition, motivated by the need for low-power inference close to the detector in future liquid argon time-projection chamber (LArTPC) experiments. Using simulation of a generic LArTPC, four Keras models are trained to classify neutral-current, muon-neutrino charged-current and electron-neutrino charged-current interactions, quantised using post-training integer quantisation and quantisation-aware training, and deployed on the Google Coral Edge TPU. Latency and energy per event are compared with those of an Intel Core i7-13650HX CPU, a consumer NVIDIA RTX 4060 GPU and a data-centre NVIDIA A100 GPU, using measured energy at different batch sizes and thread counts; the energy of the Edge TPU is estimated from its nominal power. The accuracy degradation is strongly model-dependent: InceptionV3 shows no significant loss along either pipeline, whereas the other models are substantially degraded. At batch size 1, the Edge TPU is comparable to or faster than the CPU and 1.3-6.5 times slower than the A100, while requiring 5--70 times less energy per event than the other devices; with batching, the GPUs reduce this gap to a factor of 2.6-7.2. The Edge TPU is also approximately four times cheaper than the consumer GPU and more than two orders of magnitude cheaper than the A100. Its low power per device eases deployment where power and cooling are constrained, with an additional benefit in terms of environmental impact. This paper explores possible future integrations of edge AI technologies with neutrino physics.

items.title: Vector field dark matter search with Sagnac interferometer
items.summary: We present the first calculation showing that a material-asymmetric Sagnac speed meter can improve quantum-noise-limited sensitivity to $B-L$ vector dark matter by nearly two orders of magnitude over a Fabry--Perot Michelson position meter at the low-mass end of the band. We introduce material contrast into a dual-ring interferometer to probe composition-dependent $B-L$ forces and compare the two configurations at equal incident power, input-mirror transmissivity, and cavity round-trip length. For sapphire mirrors and a one-week benchmark, the quantum-noise-only median expected $95\%$ CL upper limit reaches $1.2\times10^{-27}$ at $m_A=4.1\times10^{-14}\,\mathrm{eV}/c^2$ ($10\,\mathrm{Hz}$), a factor-$57$ improvement. This band-edge forecast assumes negligible classical noise; sensitivity at $10\,\mathrm{Hz}$ is not established for a realizable suspension and isolation system. The material-induced displacement is essentially identical in both configurations, with the gain arising from reduced low-frequency quantum backaction. These results identify speed-meter readout as a promising route to lower-mass vector-dark-matter searches.

items.title: Structured Multi-Level-Set Inversion for 3-D Electromagnetic Inverse Scattering
items.summary: Many dielectric targets encountered in 3-D electromagnetic inverse scattering exhibit piecewise-homogeneous material distributions, which provide useful structural information for inversion. To exploit this property, this paper proposes a structured multi-level-set inversion (SMLSI) method within a physics-driven neural network (PDNN) framework. Instead of directly parameterizing the contrast distribution, SMLSI represents it in terms of object support and material distribution. Multiple level-sets are mapped to soft-support functions and combined through a soft-union operation to construct the object support. The normalized contributions of these soft-support functions, together with trainable complex relative permittivities, determine the material distribution within the support. The level-set residuals are parameterized by a coordinate-based neural network, and the trainable parameters are optimized from scattered field data. Structure-aware regularization terms are introduced to promote binary object support and spatially coherent material regions while reducing material mixing and redundant activation of level-set supports. Adaptive regularization weighting is further employed to reduce the dependence on manual parameter tuning. Numerical experiments demonstrate that SMLSI improves reconstruction accuracy over direct contrast parameterization and enables the recovery of irregular 3-D geometries, closely spaced objects, and multiple material regions. Compared with CSI and $L_{2/3}$-FBE-WCIE, SMLSI achieves more accurate reconstructions on representative synthetic targets. Experimental validation using 3-D Fresnel data further demonstrates its applicability to measured scattering data.

items.title: Response of Confined Mesoscale Flames to Acoustic Forcing
items.summary: Mesoscale combustion plays a vital role in applications ranging from portable power generation to micro-propulsion systems. This study investigates the response of mesoscale flames to upstream acoustic forcing across three characteristic flame regimes: Flames with Repetitive Extinction and Ignition (FREI), Stable Flames (SF), and Propagating Flames (PF). Acoustic forcing is applied over a broad range of pressure intensities at the first harmonic of the combustor tube. At low forcing intensities, all the flame regimes exhibit oscillations at the forcing frequency without qualitative changes in their respective flame behaviours. However, as the acoustic pressure increases, all flame regimes transition to a common unsteady regime characterised by periodic ignition-extinction cycles (resembling FREI) alongside strong oscillations at the forcing frequency. This response is identified as the oscillating FREI (O-FREI) regime, in which increasing forcing intensity leads to a reduction in the mean heat release rate, an amplification of oscillations at the forcing frequency, and a drop in the Strouhal number associated with the ignition-extinction cycle. The response characteristics across all flame regimes are examined in detail and are further complemented using reduced-order mathematical models.

items.title: Active Sculpting: morphodynamics of internally stirred active vesicles
items.summary: Active flows are often confined by soft, deformable boundaries that they can push against, reshape, and in turn get reorganized by. Motivated by this interplay, we combine theory and numerical simulations to analyze the morphodynamics of an elastic vesicle enclosing a dilute suspension of extensile active particles. We model the two-dimensional vesicle as a weakly extensible elastic ring with bending rigidity, immersed in a Stokesian fluid, and describe the confined active suspension using a kinetic theory. The vesicle and the suspension are coupled hydrodynamically, through the kinematic and dynamic boundary conditions at the interface, and energetically, through a single alignment interaction that simultaneously aligns active particles with the membrane and the membrane with the particles. We show that this interaction reduces to a weak-anchoring boundary condition familiar from passive liquid crystals and derive a closed-form quiescent equilibrium state in which the nematic order in the suspension organizes into a vortex with a +1 defect core. A stability analysis of this state predicts an ordered hierarchy of activity thresholds at which successive shape modes of the vesicle are destabilized, as well as a purely passive, anchoring-driven instability of floppy vesicles. Nonlinear simulations, performed with a volume-conserving immersed boundary method, reveal that each threshold crossing gives rise to a distinct emergent state: a static spindle with boundary-pinned defects, a rotor that tank treads against its own rotation, a fluctuating spinner, and a turbulent state in which the vesicle acts as a self-stirring compartment. Beyond demonstrating how boundary deformability sculpts, and is sculpted by, confined active matter, our results open the door to study hydrodynamic interactions between such active vesicles and to use membrane fluctuations as a probe of activity of suspensions.

items.title: Static spin exchange-correlation kernel of the uniform electron gas at finite temperature
items.summary: We determine the temperature and momentum dependence of the static spin exchange--correlation kernel of the unpolarized three-dimensional uniform electron gas using variational diagrammatic Monte Carlo. The calculations cover metallic densities with Wigner--Seitz radii $r_s=1\!-\!4$ and temperatures $T/T_F=1/16\!-\!8$, where $T_F$ is the Fermi temperature. At low temperature, the calculated kernel approaches established ground-state parametrizations. Heating suppresses its Fermi-scale minimum and reduces its magnitude, while the relative momentum dependence evolves nonmonotonically through the warm-dense crossover. At the two highest temperatures studied, the spin kernel is nearly constant over $q \leq 2k_F$, where $k_F$ is the Fermi wave number. The charge kernel at $r_s=1$ retains pronounced momentum dependence under the same conditions, making a local approximation to the XC kernel more accurate in the spin channel over this interval. The directly sampled uniform response determines the XC free-energy curvature with respect to spin polarization, independently of a fitted polarization dependence. This curvature sets the interaction contribution to the free-energy cost of weak polarization and differs by several percent from the Groth--Dornheim--Bonitz parametrization at elevated temperatures. These results provide momentum-resolved reference data for finite-temperature spin-response theories and direct constraints on the spin dependence of thermal free-energy functionals.

items.title: Spectral window engineering for temporal leakage of synthetic gain waveform
items.summary: Arbitrary waveform generation enables precise engineering of optical fields. As an alternative, the synthetic wave approach has been proposed to generate virtual-gain waveforms for loss compensation. However, the achievable synthetic gain is severely limited by the finite spectral bandwidth available in realistic experiments. This imposes a rectangular spectral window, causing abrupt spectral truncation and inducing severe temporal leakage in the time domain synthetic response. Here, we introduce spectral window engineering to fundamentally resolve this limitation. By employing smooth-edged spectral filters, such as the Hann and Blackman windows, temporal leakage is pushed deeply into the late-time regime, yielding a significantly extended effective lifetime and reduced residual damping. Using a coupled plasmonic resonator platform, we experimentally validate that our windowed approach suppresses residual damping by more than a factor of two compared to the standard rectangular baseline. Our findings establish a practical and robust spectral filtering strategy to realize high efficiency synthetic gain, with promising prospects for nanodetection and advanced spectroscopy.

items.title: Intrinsic instantaneous coarse-to-fine recoverability in multiscale chaos: The Lorenz-96 system
items.summary: In multiscale chaotic systems, a central question for closure is how much of an unresolved fine-scale target can be inferred from a simultaneous coarse observation. For a specified observation-target pair, we quantify instantaneous recoverability under the invariant snapshot measure as the fraction of target variance explained by conditioning on the retained coarse variables. Evaluating this quantity across scales produces a scale-resolved recoverability map. Applied to the Lorenz-96 system across a range of forcings, the maps reveal a strongly nonuniform landscape: lower-wavenumber targets have little variance explained by the retained lower modes, while a finite band of higher modes exhibits partial recoverability once the retained scales reach the energetically active intermediate range. Recoverability onset is organized around a reference cutoff at which two retained modes can directly couple to the target through the quadratic nonlinearity, although its precise location depends on attractor statistics. Across the tested forcings, this qualitative onset structure persists while recoverability decreases, leaving a larger fraction of target variance unexplained in more strongly driven regimes. This definition identifies the maximal explained-variance fraction attainable by instantaneous deterministic models under squared loss; the estimated maps provide a scale-dependent diagnostic for closure modeling.

items.title: Augmented reality system for visualising magnetic field topology and charged-particle trajectories in magnetic fusion plasmas
items.summary: A cost-effective augmented reality (AR) system is presented for visualising three-dimensional magnetic field structures and charged-particle trajectories in magnetically confined fusion plasmas. The system presented in this study integrates an orbit-following simulation code with a marker-based AR framework using a web camera and the OpenCV library. By synchronizing the time step of the simulation with the frame rate of the camera, the trajectories are continuously updated and superimposed in real time onto the camera image. Through the interactive operation of manipulating the web camera, users can observe three-dimensional structures, such as magnetic islands, from various positions and viewing angles. Such an AR environment supports an interactive means of exploring three-dimensional spatial structures that can be difficult to interpret from two-dimensional representations alone. It also provides a common visual representation that can be shared through a display by researchers and students with diverse backgrounds in physics, engineering, and related fields. The developed system has been used in practical exercises at the JT-60SA International Fusion School, with exploratory feedback from students.

items.title: Generalized Multi-agent Social Simulation Framework
items.summary: Multi-agent social interaction has clearly benefited from Large Language Models. However, current simulation systems still face challenges such as difficulties in scaling to diverse scenarios and poor reusability due to a lack of modular design. To address these issues, we designed and developed a modular, object-oriented framework that organically integrates various base classes through a hierarchical structure, harvesting scalability and reusability. We inherited the framework to realize common derived classes. Additionally, a memory summarization mechanism is proposed to filter and distill relevant information from raw memory data, prioritizing contextually salient events and interactions. By selecting and combining some necessary derived classes, we customized a specific simulated environment. Utilizing this simulated environment, we successfully simulated human interactions on social media, replicating real-world online social behaviors. The source code for the project will be released and evolve.

items.title: Two-Way Coupled Dynamics of Quantized Vortex Bundle Formation in Spatially Periodic Normal-Fluid Turbulence
items.summary: Using fully coupled two-way simulations combining the vortex filament model with the Navier--Stokes equations, we discover that quantized vortices in superfluid $^4$He are systematically rolled up into coherent bundles within normal-fluid vortex tubes. Although co-rotating quantized vortices do not aggregate spontaneously, mutual friction with the normal fluid actively drives their bundling, directly inheriting the spatial hierarchy of classical turbulence. Mutual friction excites high-wavenumber normal-fluid vortex tubes adjacent to quantized vortices, while the superfluid forms a nested structure of thick low-wavenumber outer tubes and fine high-wavenumber inner tubes around the vortex lines. A distinct time lag between superfluid kinetic energy and dissipation fuels the energy cascade, giving rise to Kolmogorov's $k^{-5/3}$ spectrum. Crucially, bundle lifetimes are governed by the ratio of the local coupling time scale $t_\mathrm{cl}$ to the Kolmogorov dissipation time scale $τ_η$ ($t_\mathrm{cl}/τ_η< 20$), leading to enhanced thermal stability at higher temperatures. These findings establish a unified mechanism for two-fluid multiscale vortex organization.

items.title: Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relation For a Multi-Phase Alternating Renewal Random Walk
items.summary: Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relations (TURs) impose universal bounds linking current precision to entropy production in nonequilibrium systems. While general bounds like the Proesmans--Van den Broeck (PV) relation provide a broad framework, they often remain loose for processes characterized by renewal events. In this work, we derive a generalized entropic bound for current fluctuations in renewal-reward processes. By utilizing a rigorous variance decomposition within the framework of renewal-reward theory, we obtain a model-independent bound that is not only rigorous but tighter than the standard PV relation. Notably, in the linear-response regime, our bound correctly scales with the renewal rate and identifies a precision penalty arising from cycle-length fluctuations. These results provide a physically informative constraint on the precision of run-and-tumble-type dynamics and highlight the universal limits of transport in complex stochastic walkers.

items.title: Cumulus parameterization controls simulated rainfall more than microphysics, but not at heavy thresholds: a 3 * 2 factorial WRF study over the Western Himalaya
items.summary: Rainfall forecasts over the Western Himalaya remain poor, and the relative contributions of the cumulus and microphysics parameterizations to that error are not well constrained.

items.title: Two-Photon Spatial Multiplexing: Image Encoding in Gaussian Noncircularity of Light
items.summary: The search for new degrees of freedom (DoF) of light is central to advancing optical information encoding and multiplexing. Gaussian statistics are ubiquitous in nature, and here we unlock an unexpected statistical DoF in the joint noncircularity of Gaussian light. For a pair of Gaussian light fields, the covariance- and pseudocovariance-dominated two types of correlations dictate the propagation rules and the image-encoding responses, mapping optical information into coordinate-difference and coordinate-sum momentum spaces, respectively. A hybrid random-phase grating array enables the experimental preparation of noncircular Gaussian light with programmable coexistence, yielding X-shaped intensity correlations while subtly reducing the degree of second-order coherence. Two independently programmed images coexist in the same beams at identical wavelength and polarization, yet are selectively decoded through two-photon correlation geometry without physical filters. Remarkably, both images remain recoverable even when structured stray light is as intense as the signal. These results unlock a hidden statistical dimension of optical information encoding, transforming Gaussian fluctuations into a dual-channel information carrier and joint noncircularity into a programmable optical DoF.

items.title: Femtosecond all-optical polarization manipulation of harmonic generation in an anisotropic strongly coupled plasmon-epsilon-near-zero metasurface
items.summary: Ultrafast manipulation of light polarization plays a key role in modern high-speed photonics and optoelectronic operations. However, most current polarization-active modulation schemes are restricted by a limited operating wavelength range (visible to infrared), narrow-band resonant fundamental wavelength working condition, and relatively long modulation time (> 1 picosecond). Here, by taking advantage of the transient anisotropic nonlinearity of optical strong coupling between the epsilon-near-zero mode of indium tin oxide (ITO) film and polarization-selective plasmonic resonance, we achieve femtosecond polarization manipulation of broadband light that spans ultraviolet (UV) to visible region by controlling harmonic generation of the signal light under resonant pumping. We demonstrate polarization elliptic rotation of 23.3° at 407 nm for third-harmonic generation (THG) and 55.0° at 610 nm for second-harmonic generation (SHG) simultaneously within ~600 fs. In addition, the strongly coupled system can also serve as a universal femtosecond polarization modulation source, imprinting a 32.9° polarization rotation in the UV region by converting the modulation information of the fundamental signal light to that of THG light via a uniform ITO film in a cascaded configuration. Our study establishes a new paradigm for UV-based, ultrahigh-speed broadband polarization photonics with direct implications for high-speed optical information processing and programmable nonlinear photonic devices.

items.title: A compact six-beam 3D magneto-optical trap based on multifunctional metasurface chips
items.summary: Magneto-optical traps (MOTs), indispensable to cold-atom-based quantum computing and quantum precision measurement, are increasingly desired in compact and stable form. Particularly, the six-beam 3D-MOT, distinguished by symmetric geometry and superior trapping performance, finds particularly broad applications. Conventional implementations, however, rely on complex and bulky free-space optics, hindering miniaturization, practical assembly, and long-term stability. Here, we demonstrate a compact six-beam 3D-MOT system that employs two multifunctional optical metasurface chips to implement the optical-field functionalities required for cooling and trapping atoms. By combining two metasurface chips and a vacuum cell, a photonic-integrated cell module (PICM) is implemented as the core assembly and the volume is only" 73*73*107 mm^3" . In success, 1.3 * 10^3 Rb atoms are trapped and cooled to the temperature of ~183 μK. It should be noticed that the laser beam is guided to the metasurface through optical fiber, thus such fully fiber-coupled architecture enables straightforward and stable operations. We believe that this work would pave a practical route toward compact and portable 3D-MOT.

items.title: GeONet: Geometry-Encoded Operator Network for Predicting Flow in Heterogeneous Porous Media
items.summary: Rapid prediction of pressure-driven flow in microfluidic porous media is important for experimental design, tracer-test interpretation, and digital-twin development for subsurface energy and critical mineral applications. High-fidelity simulations resolve geometry-controlled flow but are computationally expensive across large geometry ensembles. Here, we introduce GeONet, a Geometry-Encoded Operator Network that predicts steady-state pressure fields by jointly representing material properties, spatial coordinates, and solid--void geometry. GeONet extends the Branch--Trunk architecture with a dedicated Leaf Network encoding the binary domain mask through multiscale features. The Branch Network represents porosity and permeability, the Trunk Network combines coordinates with local geometric descriptors and random Fourier features, and a gated DeepMixer integrates these representations to predict pressure. GeONet was trained and evaluated using 5,000 PFLOTRAN simulations of heterogeneous Reduced Complexity Platform domains, comprising nearly 30 TB of data. Comparisons with pore-scale Stokes solutions across three geometries yielded Pearson correlations of 0.987--0.991 and $R^2$ values of 0.974--0.982, supporting PFLOTRAN as reference data. Under matched partitions and two-stage hyperparameter optimization, GeONet substantially outperformed a boundary-condition-aware DeepONet baseline. Across three held-out domains, GeONet achieved NRMSE of 0.0381--0.0500, MAPE of 1.76--2.59%, and $R^2$ of 0.9673--0.9822, versus 0.1483--0.2040, 7.81--10.45%, and 0.5658--0.7126 for DeepONet, respectively. On three additional unseen geometries, GeONet achieved NRMSE of 0.0448--0.0676 and $R^2$ of 0.9511--0.9770. These results demonstrate improved accuracy, pressure-range preservation, and cross-geometry generalization through explicit geometry encoding.

items.title: Warhead Verification with Neutron Beams and Electric Cryptography
items.summary: Future arms control treaties may need to reliably verify warheads for dismantlement as part of the treaty verification process without exposing carefully guarded weapons information. Neutron Resonance Transmission Analysis has been proposed as a strategy to verify the authenticity of nuclear warheads and warhead components slated for dismantlement in an arms control verification exercise. Most actinides have resonant neutron absorption lines in the eV region, so by measuring the energy resolved transmission of neutrons and observing the resulting isotope-specific absorption lines, the authenticity of a nuclear device can be verified. To ensure acceptance of this technique by treaty partners, the measurement should minimize information learned about the warhead, including both geometric and isotopic features. Past implementations of transmission analysis acquired and compared neutron time-of-flight spectra. We have developed an analog electric cryptographic measurement proof of concept system where only counts in specific resonance energy windows are observed. The system uses discrete analog components, producing a complete data acquisition and analysis circuit. By limiting the design to easily verifiable parts, the entire apparatus is transparent to authentication and certification. The information security provided by this analog measurement technique may make it the verification basis of future ambitious arms control treaties that explicitly stipulate the dismantlement of nuclear weapons.

items.title: How Long Is the Coast of a Neuron? Resolution-Dependent Interaction Order and Computational Capacity
items.summary: Mandlebrot's coastline paradox reframes measurement as a joint property of an object and its ruler. Here we ask how observational resolution shapes the apparent structure of neural computation. We introduce a scale-indexed decomposition that separates the predictive information captured by direct dependencies from the residual outside that model family. Exact constructions show that projection can convert higher-order dependence into pairwise structure. Projection can increase the direct fraction of surviving information even as total predictive information decreases. A schematic branch-to-soma cascade grounds these effects in local coincidence detection, saturating integration and somatic mixing. Resolving organized nonlinear subunits improves approximation and raises effective representational rank. In a nested hierarchy, these gains occur without increasing information about the target. This distinction separates information availability from access by a restricted readout. A point-neuron or direct population model therefore establishes an effective description at a specified scale. It does not uniquely identify the finer computation that generated the observed relation. Which resolution is adequate depends on the observable and perturbation of interest.

items.title: A nonequilibrium-capturing unified gas-kinetic scheme I: discrete orthogonal basis construction and expansion on velocity space
items.summary: Velocity space discretization is a primary source of computational cost in deterministic methods for multiscale gas flows. A fixed velocity grid often retains redundant kinetic degrees of freedom (DOFs), particularly under near equilibrium conditions. To address this issue, this work develops a nonequilibrium-capturing formulation based on the unified gas kinetic scheme (UGKS), in which the number of kinetic DOFs adapts locally to the degree of nonequilibrium. A discrete orthogonal basis is constructed for numerical implementation, and the velocity distribution function is decomposed into an analytical local equilibrium and a basis expanded nonequilibrium component. The retained, locally adapted DOFs are evolved directly, substantially lowering computational overhead while preserving the discrete conservation of mass, momentum, and energy, as well as accurately capturing nonequilibrium states. The formulation retains the core multiscale coupling of molecular transport and collision inherent to UGKS, providing explicit and implicit schemes for unsteady and steady flows, respectively. Numerical tests across a wide range of flow speeds and rarefaction regimes (from continuum to highly rarefied) demonstrate close agreement with benchmark solutions. For unsteady flows, the explicit scheme achieves speedups of 12.64 to 58.50 over the standard UGKS. In steady state tests, only about $2\%$ of the original kinetic DOFs are required in continuum regions, accelerating each implicit iteration by a factor of 33.87. Even in the most rarefied cases, the scheme captures nonequilibrium behavior using only about $27\%$ of the original DOFs.

items.title: DiffSpecMatch: Differentiable Waveform Inverse Design with Configurable Optimization Modules for Response-Spectrum Matching of Ground Motions
items.summary: Response-spectrum matching is an underdetermined waveform inverse problem in which spectral compatibility must be achieved without uncontrolled changes in other engineering-relevant ground-motion characteristics. This study formulates the problem as differentiable waveform inverse design using a fixed SDOF dynamics engine and configurable optimization modules. An envelope-guided parameterization defines the correction waveform, while a hard projection enforces zero correction-induced terminal velocity and displacement. Differentiable SDOF responses then provide gradients for waveform optimization. Spectral fidelity and Arias-intensity accumulation are treated as adaptive objectives. Spectral feasibility, PGA, total Arias intensity, and displacement-path requirements are incorporated as constraints. The differentiable spectrum operator agrees with an exact solution of the equation of motion to within 0.002%. The complete five-damping configuration achieves a maximum spectral error of 5.00% over 375 ordinates. On a common benchmark, maximum errors of 2.61% and 8.47% are obtained for single- and multi-damping matching, respectively, while retaining the additional waveform constraints. Three-component applications further show that different engineering acceptance requirements can be accommodated through module reconfiguration without changing the forward dynamics.

items.title: A dynamic mathematical model for sub-lethal damage recovery: Integrating recovery processes into multi-target theory to visualize damage states
items.summary: Quantifying the biological effects of radiation is essential for radiotherapy and radiation protection. While research has centered on statistical analyses of experimental data, this approach often fails to elucidate underlying mechanisms, limiting the development of generalizable models. Describing time dependent phenomena, such as sub-lethal damage (SLD) recovery during fractionated irradiation, presents a particularly significant challenge for existing static models. To address this, we developed a mechanistic mathematical model that extends the classical multi-target, single-hit model by introducing explicit recovery transitions among damage states, allowing the simultaneous description of radiation-induced damage accumulation and biological recovery. We applied this model to Elkind and Sutton's classical split-dose experimental data to determine its parameters. The model reproduced the major features of split-dose survival curves for treatments with 0-, 2.5-, and 23-hour recovery intervals. We visualized the temporal changes in damage state distributions within the cell populations. These simulations provided a process-level interpretation of the characteristic shoulder-like response appearing after an inter-fraction recovery interval. Furthermore, the estimated recovery half-life was about 120 minutes, which is broadly consistent with reported timescales of DNA double-strand break repair in mammalian cells, supporting the biological interpretability of the model parameters. The proposed framework provides a simple, interpretable description of radiation-induced cell death dynamics, including SLD recovery, and may serve as a basis for the improved mechanistic modeling of radiobiological effects under different irradiation protocols.

items.title: High-level, efficient ocean modeling at all scales with Oceananigans
items.summary: We describe the user interface, governing equations, and numerical methods underpinning the ocean modeling software called "Oceananigans". Oceananigans development has been led by the Climate Modeling Alliance as part of a larger effort to build a trainable climate model with quantifiable uncertainty. Notably, Oceananigans is written in the Julia programming language, is optimized for GPUs, and can efficiently simulate all scales of ocean motion ranging from millimeter-scale turbulence in a small box to planetary-scale ocean circulation. We argue that this combination of capabilities is enabled by a design that combines a basic, easy-to-optimize, GPU-friendly structured finite volume algorithm exposed behind a high-level, programmable user interface. This design negotiates a dual mandate for highest-possible performance (to support state-of-the-art applications) and enhanced accessibility (to facilitate adoption and development). The dual mandate aims ultimately to accelerate the progress of Earth system science.

items.title: An implicit multiscale solver for steady kinetic equations based on wave-particle decomposition
items.summary: Steady kinetic computations require accurate transport on meshes that do not resolve the mean free path and efficient removal of slowly decaying macroscopic errors. We develop a closed wave-particle decomposition (WPD) and a residual-based implicit solver for this problem. The wave accumulates only the Maxwellian along a local characteristic horizon and is determined by the conservative variables; the particle carries the kinetic complement and collision remainder. Under moment compatibility, the closed system is equivalent to the kinetic equation. For the Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook and Shakhov models, a hydrodynamic expansion gives the wave and particle contributions to the Euler and Navier-Stokes fluxes. The implicit iteration couples macroscopic prediction to microscopic correction through a discrete endpoint term and synchronizes the conservative moments after each accepted correction. Its stationary states satisfy the target discrete kinetic equation independently of the iteration controls. Formal analysis gives the smooth fixed-mesh fluid limit. Linear model analysis relates convergence to the horizon-to-relaxation ratio, incomplete macroscopic solves and explicit collision remainders. One- and two-dimensional computations of a normal shock, internal flows and hypersonic external flows test these properties across rarefied and continuum regimes. The results show kinetic fidelity and substantial reductions in iteration counts and wall time relative to the conventional iterative scheme near the continuum limit. Collision-model comparisons and parameter studies support the predicted convergence mechanisms.

items.title: VEDA: Generation of 3D Molecules via Variance-Exploding Diffusion with Annealing
items.summary: Diffusion models show promise for 3D molecular generation, but face a fundamental trade-off between sampling efficiency and conformational accuracy. While flow-based models are fast, they often produce geometrically inaccurate structures, as they have difficulty capturing the multimodal distributions of molecular conformations. In contrast, denoising diffusion models are more accurate but suffer from slow sampling, a limitation attributed to sub-optimal integration between diffusion dynamics and SE(3)-equivariant architectures. To address this, we propose VEDA, a unified SE(3)-equivariant framework that combines variance-exploding diffusion with annealing to efficiently generate conformationally accurate 3D molecular structures. Specifically, our key technical contributions include: (1) a VE schedule that enables noise injection functionally analogous to simulated annealing, improving 3D accuracy and reducing relaxation energy; (2) a novel preconditioning scheme that reconciles the coordinate-predicting nature of SE(3)-equivariant networks with a residual-based diffusion objective, and (3) a new arcsin-based scheduler that concentrates sampling in critical intervals of the logarithmic signal-to-noise ratio. On the QM9 and GEOM-DRUGS datasets, VEDA matches the sampling efficiency of flow-based models, achieving state-of-the-art valency stability and validity with only 100 sampling steps. More importantly, VEDA's generated structures are remarkably stable, as measured by their relaxation energy during GFN2-xTB optimization. The median energy change is only 1.72 kcal/mol, significantly lower than the 32.3 kcal/mol from its architectural baseline, SemlaFlow. Our framework demonstrates that principled integration of VE diffusion with SE(3)-equivariant architectures can achieve both high chemical accuracy and computational efficiency.

items.title: Strong field confinement in air and enhanced optical Kerr nonlinearity of high-index star-shaped pore membrane metasurfaces
items.summary: The optical Kerr effect in high-refractive-index membrane metasurfaces patterned with a square lattice of five-pointed star-shaped pores is investigated numerically using gallium phosphide as a model material. The star geometry supports resonances with pronounced electromagnetic energy confinement, including an anapole state. The sharp tips of the star-shaped pores concentrate the electric energy density in air, exceeding that of Mie voids by a factor of seven. The effective second-order refractive index is enhanced by up to three orders of magnitude relative to bulk GaP, with the largest values obtained near the anapole resonances. The nonlinear response remains stable under polarization rotation and random misalignment of the nanoholes, indicating tolerance to fabrication imperfections. These results establish star-shaped pore lattices in freestanding membranes as a promising platform for nonlinear optics exploiting strong field confinement.

items.title: ActMOF: Mapping Reticular Synthesis through Active Learning
items.summary: Reticular chemistry allows metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) to be designed from their building units, yet their synthesis remains constrained by sparse experimental data, noisy crystallization outcomes, and the absence of benchmarks for comparing active-learning strategies. While data-driven approaches such as Bayesian optimization (BO) can improve synthesis success rates, selecting appropriate optimizers beforehand for mapping MOF crystallization landscapes remains largely empirical. Here we present ActMOF, an experiment-grounded benchmark for comparing search strategies in aluminum-carboxylate MOF synthesis. ActMOF is emulated from experimentally measured microwave syntheses with each encoded condition assigned a crystallinity index calculated based on diffraction peak intensity and full width at half-maximum. By benchmarking policies guided by Gaussian processes (GP), tree ensembles and large language models (LLM), ActMOF placed the GP family among the leading policies for active learning in sparse synthesis landscapes. It then demonstrated transferability by guiding the microwave synthesis of six reticularly related aluminum MOFs. All six campaigns gave crystalline products within a fixed budget of 12 experiments each, and established a reusable testbed for AI-driven MOF synthesis.

items.title: Wigner time delay in the $4d$ giant-resonance region of iodoalkanes
items.summary: The iodine $4d$ giant resonance provides an unusually strong and predominantly iodine-centered photoionization channel in iodoalkanes. Recent attosecond measurements by Schröder et al. [Phys. Rev. A 112, L051104 (2025)] reported pronounced, nonmonotonic, and isomer-dependent variations of the streaking-derived $4d$ photoemission delay across the molecular series. We calculate field-free molecular Eisenbud--Wigner--Smith (EWS) delays from photoionization amplitudes represented in a multicenter B-spline basis of the time-dependent density-functional theory (TDDFT). A tensor formulation is developed in which the delay for randomly oriented molecules is evaluated from the same rank-0 and rank-2 contractions that determine the cross section and anisotropy parameter. The resulting TDDFT delays of CH$_3$I, C$_2$H$_5$I, 2-iodopropane, and both calculated conformers of 1-iodopropane form a narrow bundle throughout the 90--118~eV region and closely follow atomic-I and I$^-$ reference calculations. This robustness is consistent with the similarly weak molecular dependence of the giant resonance cross section and angular distribution, but it is in marked contrast with the much larger molecular variation found by streaking experiments. The asymptotic Coulomb--laser-coupling/continuum--continuum correction is controlled mainly by the photoelectron energy and residual charge and is therefore expected to be nearly common to the iodoalkane series. This does not exclude target-specific molecular IR effects beyond the universal Coulomb term.

items.title: Physical Processes Driving Year-to-Year Surface Temperature Variability Changes in a Warming Climate
items.summary: Under anthropogenic greenhouse forcing, climate models project a decrease in year-to-year temperature variability in the mid-to-high latitudes and an increase in the tropics and subtropics. Here, we examine year-to-year temperature variability in the CESM Large Ensemble in concert with an idealized stochastic moist energy balance model (SMEBM) with effective surface heat capacity and local feedback parameter specified based on CESM. We find that the zonal-mean CESM variability change pattern largely persists after filtering out the impact of El Niño. The SMEBM largely captures this change pattern. In the SMEBM, changes in the mid-to-high latitudes are driven by changes in the effective heat capacity due to sea ice retreat, combined with changes in anomalous moist static energy convergence modulated by the polar-amplified time-mean temperature change. The CESM local feedback parameter evolves to be less stabilizing in the low latitudes, which causes tropical and subtropical variability to increase in the SMEBM.

items.title: How deterministic trajectories and their fluctuations underlie allele-frequency statistics in the strong-selection regime
items.summary: We determine statistics of allele-frequency trajectories across replicate populations. Defining $R = 2N_e|s|$ where $N_e$ is the effective population size and $s$ is the additive selection coefficient of a focal allele, we focus on strong selection which corresponds to $R \gg 1$. Strong selection does not require large selection coefficients: in populations of realistic size, it can readily arise from small selection coefficients. Our analysis concerns a biallelic locus over timescales on which mutation can be neglected. Every allele-frequency trajectory belongs to one of two absorbing classes: fixation or loss. When $R$ is large, individual allele-frequency trajectories can appear nearly deterministic. This does not imply that an approximation of allele-frequency statistics can be based on a single deterministic trajectory. For a beneficial allele, the deterministic trajectory approaches fixation, yet a non-negligible fraction of stochastic trajectories may be lost. Ignoring trajectories that achieve loss can produce severely erroneous statistics. We address this by conditioning separately on the eventual loss and eventual fixation of the focal allele. This yields an outcome-conditioned representation of a statistic. In the strong-selection regime, we apply a small-noise expansion that reasonably captures transient behaviours of statistics while recovering their exact long-time limits. We illustrate results with numerical examples for the mean allele frequency and its variance. The biological interpretation of this work is that, even under strong selection, both trajectory types are of importance. We provide a simple framework for calculating time-dependent allele-frequency statistics relevant to experimental evolution, longitudinal population-genomic data, and the dynamics of alleles driving selective sweeps.

items.title: Magnetic Reconnection Governs the Entire Lifecycle of Solar Eruptive Magnetic Flux Rope
items.summary: While magnetic flux ropes (MFRs) are widely accepted to exist prior to many solar eruptions, the physical mechanism responsible for triggering and subsequently driving their eruptions remains debated. Classical models commonly attribute eruption onset to ideal magnetohydrodynamic instabilities, particularly the torus instability, while magnetic reconnection is often regarded as a secondary process. Using high-resolution three-dimensional MHD simulations, we investigate the eruption of an MFR that forms self-consistently through flux cancellation driven by converging motions and photospheric diffusion following an initial shearing phase. The pre-eruption MFR rises quasi-statically and reaches a height where the decay index exceeds the classical torus instability threshold, yet the system continues to evolve quasi-statically without eruption. Instead, eruption begins only when the current sheet beneath the MFR becomes sufficiently thin for magnetic reconnection to set in. Increasing numerical resolution systematically delays the eruption onset, whereas the decay index at eruption onset remains nearly unchanged, demonstrating that the onset is governed by reconnection rather than torus instability. During the eruption, magnetic reconnection continuously converts surrounding sheared arcades into newly reconnected twisted flux that merges with the pre-eruption MFR and continuously to build the erupting MFR. A component-resolved analysis of the Lorentz force work further shows that the newly reconnection flux contributes predominantly to the main acceleration phase. These results demonstrate that magnetic reconnection plays a central role throughout the entire lifecycle of the eruptive MFR: it builds the MFR, directly triggers its eruption, and provides the dominant driving of the eruption.

items.title: Combined Absorption and Emission Study of Air Species in NASA EAST
items.summary: A suite of tunable diode laser absorption spectroscopy (TDLAS) diagnostics targeting rovibrational states of nitric oxide (NO) in the mid-infrared (MIR) and electronic states of atomic oxygen (O) and nitrogen (N) in the near-IR (NIR) was combined with optical emission spectroscopy (OES) for overlapping wavelengths at the NASA Electric Arc Shock Tube (EAST) facility for three selected high-temperature air experiments. Absorption features were probed at rates up to 1 MHz to provide quantitative, time-resolved measurements of temperature and species number density profiles behind incident shocks, enabling comparisons to spatially-resolved emission measurements, with the two typically agreeing within their respective uncertainties. Inferred time-histories are further compared to incident shock simulations from two one-dimensional models - one leveraging the Park two-temperature rates and the other more recent rate values - as well as the Data Parallel Line Relaxation (DPLR) code. For the two low-velocity cases (3.81 and 3.98 km/s) in which NO is probed, inferred temperatures are typically well-captured by all three models, although the NO number densities show stronger variation, agreeing better for the model with updated NO formation and dissociation rates. Finally, one high-velocity case (7.03 km/s) demonstrates the simultaneous resolution of three O-atom and six N-atom electronic states, with all states showing a steady increase in number density over time - possibly due to shock trajectory effects. Together, this combined absorption and emission study demonstrates resolution of many states of nonequilibrium air species, while directly comparing ground- and excited-state populations via the combined diagnostic strategy.

items.title: The Gompertz-Zipf city size distribution and urban allometry
items.summary: This dissertation discusses the distribution of city sizes using censuses of the Brazilian Institute for Geography and Statistics (IBGE) spanning 150 years, from 1872 to 2022, as well as the allometric scaling relation with the 2022 census data. The Gompertz distribution is fitted to the population size of less populated cities, while the Zipf power law is used to represent the cities having larger populations, with threshold varying between 20,216 and 102,857 inhabitants. The data analysis shows that the Gompertz-Zipf distribution can describe the data across all censuses, with the Gompertz parameter $B$ oscillating between $-2.39\times10^{-5}$ and $-1.49\times10^{-5}$, indicating periods with faster decreases and periods with slower decreases in the number of cities within the less populated segment as population increases, while the Zipf exponent ranges from $a=3.61\pm0.09$ in 1872 to $a=2.28\pm0.02$ in 2022.
