Through these and other modifications to the asymptotic analysis argument, the theoretical statistics for the run length, run time, and velocity of the motor-cargo ensemble can be brought into reasonable agreement with direct model simulations of two-motor ensembles consisting of kinesin-1 and kinesin-2. Additionally, we propose a new data fitting approach to obtain a double-exponential parameterization for the detachment rate of a motor as a function of the momentary force on its tether to the cargo, which is continuous at low load. Such a modified parameterization is needed to avoid artifacts in theoretical modeling of intracellular transport.

items.title: RNAGenScape: Property-Guided, Optimized Generation of mRNA Sequences with Manifold Langevin Dynamics
items.summary: Generating property-optimized mRNA sequences is central to applications such as vaccine design and protein replacement therapy, but remains challenging due to limited data, complex sequence-function relationships, and the narrow space of biologically viable sequences. Generative methods that drift away from the data manifold can yield sequences that fail to fold, translate poorly, or are otherwise nonfunctional. We present RNAGenScape, a property-guided manifold Langevin dynamics framework for mRNA sequence generation that operates on a learned manifold of real data. By performing iterative local optimization constrained to this manifold, RNAGenScape preserves favorable computational viability proxies, accesses reliable guidance, and discourages excursions into regions poorly supported by the training data. The framework integrates three components: (1) an autoencoder jointly trained with a property predictor to learn a property-organized latent manifold, (2) a denoising autoencoder that projects updates back onto the manifold, and (3) a property-guided Langevin dynamics procedure that performs optimization along the manifold. Across three real-world mRNA datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size, RNAGenScape increases median oracle-predicted property gain by up to 267% and success rate by up to 31%, while maintaining good biological viability proxy measures and achieving competitive inference efficiency compared to existing generative approaches.

items.title: Predicting Cognitive Tasks from Single-Channel EEG through Task-Semantic Alignment
items.summary: Studies of data scaling in electroencephalography (EEG) and related noninvasive recordings suggest that simple wearable devices could eventually reveal more about cognitive states. However, publicly available EEG data are difficult to combine. Different laboratories record different tasks, participants, and devices. Task-agnostic self-supervised learning can exploit such data, but representations learned only with EEG signals have not consistently produced feature representations that are directly effective for decoding the cognitive state. We therefore aimed to incorporate task information by embedding experimental instructions, stimuli and response demands in a common semantic space, and trained an EEG encoder to align signals from a single anterior--posterior differential channel with those task vectors. This framework supports zero-shot prediction without target-condition calibration and few-shot prediction using labeled samples. On a reserved ten-class evaluation, the highest observed zero-shot balanced accuracy was 30.13% (chance 10%). In a separate developmental few-shot experiment, balanced accuracy reached 34.47% using 16 labeled EEG examples per class from another participant, and 74.99% using examples from the test participant's own task recording. Our experiments suggest that training models on datasets with multiple tasks per participant appeared useful, whereas adding datasets containing only one or a few tasks sometimes reduced established performance despite broader task coverage. These exploratory results suggest that EEG datasets that repeat varied cognitive tasks and everyday activities within the same individuals across days, devices and independent studies would be particularly useful for training an EEG foundation model for predicting cognitive states.

items.title: Multi-Agent Learning of Reactive Strategies in Iterated Games
items.summary: Learning agents, whether humans or algorithms, adapt to one another rather than to a fixed environment. Selfish learning need not produce a good outcome for the group, especially when learners face a social dilemma. The iterated prisoner's dilemma (IPD) is the classical example, but it is usually studied in populations of agents who imitate successful strategies. Here, we instead study selfish gradient ascent learners on the two-dimensional space of reactive strategies. A reactive strategy is described by two continuous traits: reciprocity, the chance of cooperating after the co-player cooperates, and forgiveness, the chance of cooperating after the co-player defects. Each learner updates its strategy in the direction that most rapidly improves its payoff against all other learners, by an amount governed by its learning rate. We show that heterogeneity in learning rates can qualitatively change the long-term outcome: a population with uniform learning rates converges to always-defect (ALLD), whereas a population with variable learning rates approaches generous-tit-for-tat (GTFT), which produces nearly optimal collective payoffs. In simulations, every population passes through a transient state of minimal forgiveness, in which the distribution of reciprocity determines the outcome. Variable learning rates promote cooperation because slow learners preserve high reciprocity until the population reaches this state. We prove sufficient conditions on the distribution of reciprocity for convergence to ALLD or to tit-for-tat (TFT). Variable learning rates also allow cooperation to recover from perturbation, which is provably impossible under uniform learning. These results suggest that purely selfish and myopic learning can produce persistent cooperation provided the population has intrinsic variability in learning rates.

items.title: Bayesian adaptive design for neural recruitment curves
items.summary: Nonlinear response models remain ubiquitous across disciplines with recruitment curves describing muscle response to neural stimulation. Conventional acquisition methods typically rely on static uniform sampling, requiring many stimuli, while adaptive threshold-hunting designs such as ML-PEST forfeit accurate characterization of the overall curve. We present a Bayesian adaptive design that uses posterior uncertainty over curve parameters to propose stimuli that maximize information gain across the full recruitment curve. We additionally implement a focused acquisition method that can target arbitrary subset of curve parameters, which we use to evaluate and interpret our design. In simulations, our design outperforms uniform sampling in recovering threshold while matching ML-PEST, and outperforms ML-PEST in predictive curve accuracy while matching uniform. It likewise matches our threshold-focused acquisition, suggesting our design doesn't trade off threshold estimation for recovering the curve. We further show data collected using our design yields greater power when detecting a change in threshold in intervention studies. Our design proposes the next stimulus within 5 seconds, making it feasible for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) experiments. Finally, we validate our design in TMS experiments and provide a library for Python, called onMEP, for online acquisition of neural recruitment curves.

items.title: Ensemble-Based Modelling of Optogenetic Bioprocesses under Phototoxicity
items.summary: Optogenetics enables methanol-free protein production in the yeast $\textit{Komagataella phaffii}$ using light as a control input, facilitated by the blue-light-responsive transcription factor EL222. This opens the door to more programmable protein production in the food and biopharmaceutical industries. However, excessive illumination can inhibit growth and protein accumulation in some of these engineered cell factories. Previous hybrid modelling used black-box regression across sparsely sampled conditions to infer light-dependent kinetic parameters, without explicitly representing intracellular regulation. Here, we develop a multiscale mechanistic model linking EL222 activation, transcription, and translation to protein, biomass, and substrate dynamics. A latent light-associated stress state represents photoinhibitory effects on growth, transcription, and translation. An ensemble-based parameter-estimation strategy combines repeated global-local optimisation with screening for parameter sets supporting locally stable intracellular steady states under specified light conditions. Using available batch data for yeast-enhanced green fluorescent protein production in a $\textit{K. phaffii}$ strain carrying eight EL222 gene copies, the ensemble-mean predictions captured the main experimental trends in protein accumulation and growth across six constant light intensities. Parameter variability was propagated to time-course predictions, providing an empirical assessment of parameter-related uncertainty. Wider prediction bands coincided with less complete experimental coverage of the growth phases. Overall, the framework provides a mechanistic basis for future model-based optimisation and control of optogenetic bioprocesses under phototoxicity.

items.title: A mathematical model for fitness effects on viral persistence
items.summary: Persistent viral infections arise from complex interactions between viral replication, host cell responses, and ongoing viral evolution. A general framework linking viral fitness to persistence dynamics is lacking. Here, we develop for the first time a mathematical model of viral persistence that takes into consideration viral fitness variations. Essential to the model is the partition of the classical fitness parameter into three components: replicative, infective, and dispersal fitness. The model was initially inspired by a new experiment on hepatitis C virus (HCV) persistence, established in human hepatoma cells, also reported in this work. This experiment documents two strikingly different viral trajectories depending on the initial replicative fitness of the viral population used to establish persistence. The dynamical model describes the interactions among uninfected cells, infected cells, and infectious virions, and it incorporates, through a continuum, two alternative mechanisms of viral release from cells: budding and lysis. Analysis of the model reveals that viral fitness parameters organise infection outcomes into distinct dynamical regimes. Low replicative and dispersal fitness values lead to viral extinction, whereas high values enable persistence through either stable coexistence or recurrent infection waves. The space of fitness discloses a hierarchy among these parameters, with replicative and dispersal fitness being able to trigger important shifts in the outcome of the infection as opposed to infective fitness. The model identifies trade-offs between replication and dispersal that shape viral production and predicts slow dynamical regimes in which infection may persist despite low detectable viral loads. It provide candidates mechanisms capable of generating the persistence patterns observed experimentally.

items.title: Full Lyapunov Spectra of Random Neural Networks, Part I: Finite-Time and Asymptotic Theory
items.summary: We develop a dynamical mean-field framework for the full finite-time and stationary asymptotic Lyapunov spectra of random recurrent neural networks. At finite observation time, an exact log-determinant representation of tangent-propagator singular values leads to a closed-contour matrix Dyson equation for the smoothed spectral tail. In the stationary setting, a cocycle representation yields an operator equation for the asymptotic cumulative spectrum. Both formulations retain complete local gain histories and the repeated action of quenched connectivity. Direct singular-value calculations and network QR spectra support the predictions in the regimes examined, with sampling uncertainty and numerical cutoffs assessed separately. The stationary equation also recovers the known maximal exponent, and controlled gain-history replay illustrates how temporal correlations redistribute instability. This work was carried out in collaboration with ChatGPT 5.6 Sol. Toward the end of preparation we became aware of David G. Clark's contemporaneous work, \emph{Lyapunov spectrum of random neural networks}[arXiv:2610.12426], which reports overlapping mean-field results for the full Lyapunov spectrum using a cavity approach.

items.title: Multilateral governance of invasive alien species management: An ecological-economic model with Allee effect
items.summary: Invasive alien species (IAS) generate substantial ecological and economic damages that often transcend political boundaries, creating strong incentives for coordinated management. We develop a two-region ecological-economic model of IAS control that integrates prevention and eradication measures with population dynamics characterized by logistic growth and an Allee effect. We derive analytical results on the interaction between ecological thresholds and strategic behaviour and compare outcomes under cooperation (central planner) and non-cooperation (open loop Nash equilibrium and Markovian Nash equilibrium). We show that, under realistic control costs, neither prevention nor eradication can eliminate invasive populations in finite time, and complete prevention of cross-border spread is generally not optimal. In the absence of an Allee effect, the zero-population equilibrium is unstable, implying long-run persistence of the invasive species. By contrast, the presence of an Allee effect fundamentally alters system dynamics by making extinction locally stable and creating a basin of attraction within which eradication becomes feasible. This finding highlights the economic significance of ecological thresholds and demonstrates how delays in management can shift populations beyond critical levels, after which eradication is unlikely regardless of subsequent control efforts. Numerical simulations further show that cooperative management expands the set of initial conditions leading to eradication and consistently reduces aggregate social costs relative to decentralized management. The results provide a formal rationale for rapid intervention, precautionary regulation, and stronger multilateral cooperation in IAS management, particularly in jurisdictions such as the European Union where listing and control actions may be delayed pending evidence of harm.

items.title: Spin-Based Modeling of Perception as Emergent from contextualized Internal Evaluation
items.summary: We develop a microscopic model of perception of an interoceptive sensation in which spin-like variables encode an organism's internal evaluation of embodied vital norms associated with the sensation. Spins can take positive, negative, or neutral values. These local valorizations interact on a lattice embedded in the environmental context, and their collective configuration gives rise to a macroscopic perceptual state. By applying a coarse-graining procedure to a family of symmetric spin models, we derive a macroscopic Landau-type functional that makes explicit the mechanism by which key phenomenological features of perception, emerge from microscopic evaluative interactions. A central result is that the inclusion of a neutral evaluative state fundamentally alters the structure of the perceptual landscape, enhancing entropy, lowering the critical threshold, and increasing sensitivity to contextual input. These results establish a principled link between microscopic evaluative processes and large-scale perceptual organization, offering a flexible framework for integrating perceptual regulation and neurobiological modeling. The model integrates notions of neuroscience and cognitive science using the formalism of condensed matter field theory and providing novel theoretical insights and experimental predictions for conditions such as mental disorders and chronic pain.

items.title: Amortised Global Sensitivity Analysis of Pharmacokinetic models for Simulated Clinical Trials
items.summary: Pharmacokinetic and pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic models are used in simulated clinical trials to compare dosing protocols and patient groups before a trial is run. Distinct virtual patient cohorts, representing renal impairment, obesity and overdosage, can impose different input distributions on the same model. Global sensitivity analysis (GSA) identifies which uncertain inputs drive the cohort's predictions, but a direct analysis incurs its full computational cost for every cohort. An alternative accounting is proposed here: a single surrogate is trained on an input envelope wide enough to contain every cohort, each cohort is then analysed using that surrogate, and the reported quantity is the number of cohorts at which the surrogate route has cost fewer mechanistic evaluations than the direct route. The study tests three GSA methods: variance-based GSA, Morris screening and optimal transport. It covers four PK and PK/PD models with seven to twenty-three free inputs, 21 cohorts and five surrogates. Every estimate is scored against a converged mechanistic solution obtained with its own method, and all costs are expressed in mechanistic model evaluations. The parameter ranking is recovered at low cost: gradient-boosted trees reconstruct it on 20 of the 21 cohorts and cost fewer evaluations to train than one direct cohort analysis, on all four models, at break-even counts between 0.02 and 0.14 cohorts. Amortisation is fastest at the highest dimensions, where each direct variance-based sample of a $D$-input model requires $D+2$ evaluations while the training budget does not scale accordingly. Recovering absolute index values is harder, and fewer surrogates manage it as inputs grow: two of the five surrogates fail at fifteen inputs, where the gradient-boosted trees and the Gaussian process still succeed, and at twenty-three inputs no surrogate succeeds on a majority of cohorts.

items.title: Bayesian Uncertainty Quantification of Breast-Cancer Pathology AI Agreement under Reader- and Annotation-Condition-Dependent Reference Labels
items.summary: Human reference labels used to evaluate medical AI can vary across readers and annotation workflows. We quantified agreement of a fixed pathology AI system with a future qualified reader without treating inferred consensus as error-free biological truth. Linked Evaluation and Unbiased NuCLS multirater data were analyzed using a fixed external HoVer-Net decision vector. The selected frame contained 1,144 anchors, 52 fields of view, five slides/patients, and five primary readers. The target was fixed-AI agreement with a future reader, with descriptive contrast $Δ=θ_E-θ_U$. Analyses included raw agreement and iMRMC benchmarks, reader-only and shared-detectability Bayesian models, structural sensitivities, adversarial simulations, and predictive assessment. Among 5,188 reader-anchor pairs observed in both conditions, 19.62% changed AI-agreement state, while raw agreement was 0.5466 in Unbiased and 0.5473 in Evaluation. The reader-only model gave $Δ=-0.0008$ (95% CrI, $-0.0033$ to $0.0008$), and the shared-detectability model gave $Δ\approx0$ ($-0.0140$ to $0.0127$). Across structural perturbations, absolute agreement ranged from 0.420 to 0.646 in Unbiased and 0.409 to 0.640 in Evaluation. Frozen adversarial simulations met the comparative-stability criterion (median $R=0.295$; 14/16 model-scenario cells had $R<1$). Held-out-AI prediction supported shared predictive information, but varied by slide composition. The Evaluation-minus-Unbiased contrast was comparatively stable, whereas absolute agreement was structurally sensitive. These findings do not establish equivalence, causal assistance effects, biological accuracy, or new-patient transportability. Evaluations using variable human references should report reader population, selected frame, observation mechanism, and structural sensitivity.

items.title: TempoBridge: Source-Conditioned Flow Matching with Optimal Transport Couplings for Single-Cell Population Transitions
items.summary: Destructive single-cell measurements provide unpaired population snapshots rather than observations of the same cells across conditions. Local cell states and transition requests may also be insufficient to distinguish responses across source populations. We introduce TempoBridge, a common source-conditioned transport formulation for temporal, genetic, and chemical population transitions. Source cells initialize latent transport and provide a fixed empirical population summary. The velocity field receives this summary alongside the evolving cell state, flow time, and a structured transition descriptor. Minibatch optimal transport (OT) supplies couplings only for conditional flow-matching training paths; inference requires neither target expression nor OT computation. On held-out donors, TempoBridge achieves an Energy distance of 0.129 versus 0.144 for scGen. Genetic mean-expression $L_2$ error is 2.261 versus 3.156 for scGPT-scratch under Seen 2/2. On held-out compounds, condition-averaged drug-effect correlation is 0.598 versus 0.561 for the CellFlow adapter. Temporal ablations show higher mean distributional error after removing source context, replacing optimal transport with random pairing, or replacing flow matching with static residual regression. Together, these results demonstrate the predictive utility of a common source-conditioned transport formulation across held-out donors, gene combinations, and compounds.

items.title: manylp: reproducible, exact, and batched linear programming for genome-scale dynamic flux balance analysis
items.summary: Dynamic flux balance analysis (dFBA) and its community, spatial and ensemble variants predict microbial metabolism by solving one linear program (LP) per species and time step, often 10^6 to 10^8 LPs per study. These LPs share their constraint matrix and objective and differ only in their bounds, yet general-purpose solvers treat each one independently, and GPU first-order solvers struggle with the degenerate, badly scaled matrices of genome-scale models. Moreover, metabolic optima are usually faces rather than vertices, so solvers return arbitrary flux vectors and dFBA predictions depend on the solver used. We present manylp, a batched solver for such bounds-parametric LP families that returns certified vertex solutions. Building on the bunching technique of stochastic programming, manylp caches optimal bases and certifies whole batches with one dense matrix product per basis on CPUs or GPUs; LPs outside the cached critical regions are re-solved by a warm-started lexicographic dual simplex, and new bases are propagated across the batch. Each LP is certified optimal and unique under a lexicographic flux rule, or infeasible, in independent double-precision arithmetic. On a genome-scale dFBA workload, manylp certified 47,889 LPs per second on a CPU, 12 to 33 times faster than HiGHS, Gurobi, FICO Xpress, GLPK and OR-Tools (32 processes), and reached 682,000 LPs per second on one GPU for community ensembles, needing 76 simplex solves for 94.6 million LPs. Integrated into the muODE simulator, it accelerated single trajectories 84-fold and 16-member ensembles 635-fold, and made adaptive Runge-Kutta integration affordable, reducing biomass errors 83-fold. Integrating 49 equally optimal flux policies in one batched run showed that alternative optima change predicted acetate 4.2-fold and shift community composition. manylp is open source: https://github.com/cumbof/manylp.

items.title: Consistent and scalable detection and comparison of spatial patterns
items.summary: Spatial omics maps molecular features within tissues to study their organization across biological contexts, including disease and development. Interpreting these maps requires distinguishing patterns from noise and comparing them across samples. Yet pattern detection remains unresolved, and comparisons based on regional summaries lose spatial detail. Here we show that spatial frequency provides a common basis for detecting and comparing these patterns. Our framework, SONIC, unifies spatial detection tests through a common quadratic form, establishes conditions for reliable detection and explains how kernel choice determines sensitivity to different spatial patterns. It also separates changes in spatial organization from changes in overall abundance without aligning tissues. Fast, memory-efficient algorithms make detection and comparison practical across large datasets. Applying SONIC, we identify plaque-associated responses in Alzheimer's disease and differences in the spatial expression of blood-clotting genes between glioma subtypes. We further construct a gene-centric atlas that traces changes in spatial expression through mouse and human embryogenesis and supports retrieval of related patterns across species. These results extend spatial analysis from identifying individual patterns to following their changes across anatomically different tissues. Together, SONIC establishes a shared language for integrating molecular maps across studies and technologies.

items.title: DyssomniaNN: Multi-Scale Spiking Neural Modeling of Human Sleep Disorders and Perceived Restedness
items.summary: Clinical sleep medicine repeatedly documents profound divergences between objective sleep duration and subjective daytime impairment, notably exemplified by sleep state misperception in paradoxical insomnia and boundary instability in narcolepsy type 1. Here, we present DyssomniaNN: a multi-scale biophysical computational framework coupling Borbély's two-process regulation of sleep homeostasis and circadian drive with Saper's hypothalamic reciprocal flip-flop circuit and a recurrent corticothalamic leaky integrate-and-fire spiking neural network. We formalize five clinical cohorts across an identical 72-hour photoperiod: healthy control, circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder (delayed-phase), chronic insomnia, paradoxical insomnia, and narcolepsy type 1. The synthetic local field potential converges closely with empirical human electroencephalography spectra from the PhysioNet Sleep-EDF database across all canonical frequency bands (spectral mean absolute error of 0.33--0.35). Furthermore, we introduce the Well-Rested Index to quantify restorative efficacy. Simulations reveal that sleep duration fails to predict restorative recovery: paradoxical insomnia achieves normal total sleep time (21.15 h) yet yields low restoration (37.6%) from unsuppressed cortical beta-band intrusion, whereas hypocretin deficiency in narcolepsy produces severe nocturnal fragmentation (781 min of wake after sleep onset) and 35 sleep-onset rapid eye movement periods. DyssomniaNN provides an in silico platform for mechanistic sleep research and virtual neuropharmacology.

items.title: PhySeqNet: physics-informed fluorescent foci detection for BARseq spatial transcriptomics
items.summary: BARseq enables spatially resolved gene-expression profiling across intact tissue, but its sensitivity depends on accurate detection and decoding of dense fluorescent rolonies. Existing spot-calling approaches can be conservative where signals overlap, while supervised deep learning is limited by the lack of reliable manual ground truth in real tissue images. Here we present PhySeqNet, a physics-informed deep learning framework for annotation-free fluorescent foci detection in BARseq. PhySeqNet trains U-Net detectors entirely on semi-synthetic images generated from an instrument-matched optical model combined with real sample-free experimental noise, and is integrated into pyBARseq, a modular Python pipeline for BARseq analysis. PhySeqNet achieved high detection performance on held-out simulated data across wavelength bands. On real tissue images, where ground truth is unavailable, we evaluated detections by forward-model reconstruction: PhySeqNet with conservative barcode-aware non-maxima suppression (NMSB) achieved higher reconstruction fidelity (NCC and MS-SSIM) than the BarDensr single-shot estimator, tuned classical spot detectors, and a pretrained deep-learning detector. In the analyzed brain section, PhySeqNet with NMSB yielded a median of 51 counts per cell versus 47 for BarDensr, with a similar number of genes detected per cell. The recovered transcripts produced spatial expression patterns qualitatively consistent with Allen MERFISH reference data and preserved cell-type composition after scANVI label transfer. These results show that physics-informed simulation can train practical, annotation-free detectors that improve BARseq sensitivity without disrupting downstream biological interpretation.

items.title: Robust Machine Learning for Regulatory Sequence Modeling under Biological and Technical Distribution Shifts
items.summary: Robust machine learning for regulatory genomics is studied under biologically and technically induced distribution shifts. Deep convolutional and attention based models achieve strong in distribution performance on DNA regulatory sequence prediction tasks but are usually evaluated under i.i.d. assumptions, even though real applications involve cell type specific programs, evolutionary turnover, assay protocol changes, and sequencing artifacts. We introduce a robustness framework that combines a mechanistic simulation benchmark with real data analysis on a massively parallel reporter assay (MPRA) dataset to quantify performance degradation, calibration failures, and uncertainty based reliability. In simulation, motif driven regulatory outputs are generated with cell type specific programs, PWM perturbations, GC bias, depth variation, batch effects, and heteroscedastic noise, and CNN, BiLSTM, and transformer models are evaluated. Models remain accurate and reasonably calibrated under mild GC content shifts but show higher error, severe variance miscalibration, and coverage collapse under motif effect rewiring and noise dominated regimes, revealing robustness gaps invisible to standard i.i.d. evaluation. Adding simple biological structural priors motif derived features in simulation and global GC content in MPRA improves in distribution error and yields consistent robustness gains under biologically meaningful genomic shifts, while providing only limited protection against strong assay noise. Uncertainty-aware selective prediction offers an additional safety layer that risk coverage analyses on simulated and MPRA data show that filtering low confidence inputs recovers low risk subsets, including under GC-based out-of-distribution conditions, although reliability gains diminish when noise dominates.

items.title: Beyond Discrimination: Evaluating Probability Calibration in Radiomics-Image Fusion for Renal Cell Carcinoma Classification
items.summary: Reliable probability estimates are important for the clinical interpretation of machine-learning classifiers, yet radiomics--image fusion models for renal cell carcinoma (RCC) are commonly evaluated primarily by discrimination. Using 396 patients from the KiTS23 dataset, we evaluated whether adding radiomics to four image-model families improved probabilistic performance in addition to discrimination. Seventeen individual models and four probability-average ensembles were assessed using discrimination, probability calibration, and proper scoring measures. Across 12 matched image-only versus fusion comparisons, AUC and AP improved in all 12, while Brier score and negative log likelihood (NLL) improved in 11 of 12 and expected calibration error (ECE) in eight of 12. The 3D MedVAE gated-fusion model achieved the strongest overall individual-model profile. Probability averaging across concatenation, cross-attention, and gated fusion produced favourable point estimates across all five primary metrics relative to image-only models in all four families, although paired-bootstrap support was stronger for Brier score and NLL than for ECE. These findings show that radiomics--image fusion can improve probabilistic prediction quality beyond discrimination, while calibration behaviour varies across image architectures and fusion strategies. We show that our proposed probability-average ensemble models improve discrimination and calibration simultaneously across all architectures in the study.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Systems Biology Reconstruction of Diabetic Bone Marrow Dysfunction
items.summary: This study aimed to reconstruct a regulatory network suitable for systems biology analysis of diabetic bone marrow. Three artificial intelligence large language models independently analysed 18 Discovery and 43 Validation publications. Investigator guided integration produced a frozen network of 62 biological entities and 79 directed interactions. Open source software Gephi created a visual representation before and after main node removal. The plausibility of the reconstructed interactions was tested against independent curated knowledge resources, including the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes, connectomeDB2025, Reactome, and Gene Ontology. Further analysis examined physiological correspondence, missing edge sensitivity, and graph constrained interrogation. Functional modules encompassed endothelial perivascular support, stem cell retention and trafficking, neural circadian regulation, inflammatory myelopoiesis, metabolic stress, and epigenetic regulation. They intersected through shared effects on endothelial function and stem cell behaviour. The endothelium was the principal connecting node. Computational removal of the endothelial node increased network fragmentation and diameter, while average directed path length remained essentially unchanged. External resources supported 60/79 interactions (75.9%); 19 remained unresolved, with none classified as contradictory. Complementary assessments supported biological plausibility and faithful interrogation of the reconstructed network. This investigator led dialogue with artificial intelligence provides a foundation for a systems level understanding of diabetic bone marrow dysfunction. The approach may facilitate the generation of testable hypotheses and the identification of mechanistic targets for coordinated restoration of disrupted niche interactions.

items.title: Leaky protection reveals three patterns in the relative advantages of vaccination strategies across transmission intensity
items.summary: Targeted vaccination often prioritizes individuals who contribute most to transmission. However, this rationale may change under leaky protection, whereby vaccination reduces susceptibility at each exposure rather than fully preventing infection. Here, we use a survey-derived individual-level exposure framework for 2,279 residents to simulate infection dynamics across ranges of transmission intensity and vaccine efficacy. We compare two vaccination strategies: the high-exposure strategy (prioritizing highly exposed individuals) and the oldest-first strategy (prioritizing older individuals). As transmission intensity changes, we identify three patterns in the relative advantages of these two strategies. At low transmission, the high-exposure strategy outperforms the oldest-first strategy in reducing both epidemic peak size and final infection proportion. At intermediate transmission, it lowers epidemic peak size but increases final infection proportion, revealing a trade-off between these metrics. At high transmission, differences between the strategies narrow, and the oldest-first strategy has a slight advantage for both metrics. Overall, our findings highlight the importance of considering vaccine failure mode when evaluating vaccination policies under different transmission dynamics.

items.title: EEG Entrainment to Non-Speech Rhythmic Patterns Associated with Dimensions of Language Performance
items.summary: Developmental dyslexia (DLX) affects 5-12% of the global population and impairs learning to read. Its biological basis, particularly the difficulties observed in oral phonological tasks, remains debated. Entrainment, the coupling of brain oscillations to speech rhythms, is essential for encoding phonological representations. We investigated whether brain entrainment to non-speech rhythms could predict DLX in 48 participants listening to white noise amplitude-modulated at rates matching Spanish speech units. Phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) analysis of electroencephalography (EEG) signals yielded accurate DLX prediction for the 40 Hz stimulus using the Heights Ratio PAC measure (balanced accuracy 0.929, p = 0.0069, in the best case), indicating a stronger phonemic entrainment deficit in dyslexic individuals. Regression analysis in control (CTL) participants showed a strong dependence between reading performance scores and greater entrainment in language-associated brain regions. In particular, participants with poorer phonemic awareness, reading comprehension, or rapid automatized naming showed greater right-hemisphere entrainment to the 40 Hz stimulus. This finding adds evidence for the hemispheric compensatory mechanisms hypothesized in the literature. In conclusion, our methodology identifies dyslexia-specific entrainment patterns near language-associated brain regions, together with compensatory entrainment in right-hemisphere areas.

items.title: Decoding Alignment without Encoding Alignment: A critique of similarity analysis in neuroscience
items.summary: RSA and CKA are standard metrics for comparing neural representations across brain regions, organisms, and deep learning models. We demonstrate a fundamental weakness: these decoding-based metrics are insensitive to encoding manifold topology---the internal functional organization of a neural population. In a controlled MNIST experiment, RSA, CKA, and Procrustes $R^2$ remain statistically unchanged when encoding topology is causally manipulated via an auxiliary clustering loss, while the two model populations differ significantly in attribution patterns, weight-graph assortativity, and out-of-distribution robustness. Across biological systems and machine learning models, similar decoding behavior can arise from small, non-representative subpopulations, and alignment metrics are insensitive to encoding manifold topology even when it is fundamentally altered. These findings bear directly on mechanistic interpretability: standard alignment metrics cannot distinguish whether two networks share the same computational circuits or merely produce indistinguishable aggregate outputs. We propose encoding manifolds and Gromov-Wasserstein distance as complementary diagnostics for any decoding-based similarity claim, and provide a Neural Manifold Explorer tool at https://johannesbertram.github.io/FNN_Manifolds/index.html for further experimentation.

items.title: Beyond Anxiety and Avoidance: A Dynamic Feedback-Regulation Framework for Adult Romantic Attachment
items.summary: Adult attachment is commonly represented by attachment anxiety and avoidance, but these person-level dimensions do not by themselves specify how momentary relational conditions are perceived, compared with desired conditions, translated into action, and updated after interpersonal feedback. We present the Attachment Regulation and Control (ARC) framework as an integrative feedback-regulation account that makes these temporal assumptions explicit and empirically testable. In ARC, control refers to feedback-based regulation toward relational goals in the control-theoretic sense, not interpersonal dominance, coercion, or a generalized need for control. ARC does not claim a novel control-system architecture. Instead, it synthesizes established control-theoretic attachment ideas, secure-base representations, perceived partner responsiveness, relational discrepancy, dyadic regulation, and recovery into a parsimonious sequence for adult romantic relationships: perceived relational state, desired relational state, discrepancy, regulatory action, partner feedback, state updating, and recovery. The framework treats the discrepancy score itself as a falsifiable modeling restriction by comparing it with perceived-state-only, unconstrained perceived-plus-desired-state, and asymmetric discrepancy alternatives. Attachment anxiety and avoidance form core regulation moderators. Secure-base representation is a candidate requiring incremental prediction of recovery outcomes. Mentalized affectivity and regulation flexibility remain optional moderators, while adult disorganization is an independent extension outcome.

items.title: MORAD: Reinforcement Learning with Multi-Objective Rewards for RNA Inverse Design
items.summary: We introduce MORAD, an online reinforcement learning framework for backbone-conditioned RNA diffusion models that trains a single shared policy across diverse target backbones. Structure-conditioned RNA inverse design seeks nucleotide sequences compatible with a target three-dimensional backbone, yet existing reinforcement learning approaches either optimize a separate policy for each target backbone or rely on offline preference optimization, leaving online post-training of a reusable backbone-conditioned model largely unexplored. MORAD combines backbone-conditioned group sampling, group-relative reward normalization, and a forward-process diffusion objective. Beyond existing RL rewards that primarily target tertiary structural quality, MORAD jointly optimizes six measurements spanning tertiary geometry, base pairing, ensemble behavior, and sequence composition. To aggregate these heterogeneous objectives despite differences in scale and optimization direction, MORAD maps each measurement to a bounded desirability score and combines them with a weighted geometric mean. Compared with a tertiary-structure-only reward, this multi-objective formulation improves 10 of the 11 evaluation metrics that have a preferred direction. Applied to pretrained RIDE, MORAD improves GDT-TS by 16.0% (from 0.3300 to 0.3827) and pairing MCC by 19.4% (from 0.6110 to 0.7295), while reducing normalized ensemble defect by 27.5% (from 0.3906 to 0.2830). On the test set, MORAD outperforms RiboDiffusion, gRNAde, and RDesign across tertiary structural accuracy, secondary-structure pairing, and thermodynamic quality, establishing a new state of the art in structure-conditioned RNA inverse design.

items.title: Excitability across scales: a unifying EI model
items.summary: Neuronal excitability is commonly modeled using different principles at the cellular and population scales, making it difficult to study how microscopic mechanisms shape macroscopic activity. We introduce a spatiotemporal excitatory-inhibitory (EI) model that unifies these scales through a common mixed-feedback architecture. The model retains the conductance-based circuit structure of Hodgkin-Huxley models and describes intrinsic and synaptic currents through memductances whose temporal and spatial voltage dependence encodes dynamics at the relevant scale. In its minimal form, temporal excitability arises from fast excitatory feedback opposed by slower inhibitory feedback, while spatial excitability arises from short-range excitation opposed by longer-range inhibition, recovering the core lateral-inhibition motif of Amari neural fields. We show that combining these mechanisms gives rise to population excitability in strongly heterogeneous populations. In particular, the model generates population spikes that are localized in both space and time and possess population-level scales distinct from those of individual neuronal spikes, despite substantial cell-to-cell parameter variability. We then show that both intrinsic temporal excitability and spatial synaptic feedback are required for coherent mean-field events and robust spatiotemporal population rhythms. Finally, selective modulation of memductances in a subset of the population tunes the frequency of the population rhythm, illustrating how changes at the cellular scale can shape macroscopic dynamics. By separating circuit architecture from modeling scale, the proposed framework provides a physically interpretable approach to analyzing and designing neuronal excitability across scales.

items.title: On estimating the effective sample size of phylogenetic trees in an autocorrelated chain
items.summary: Estimating the effective sample size (ESS) is fundamental in Bayesian phylogenetic inference to account for autocorrelation in MCMC samples. While methods for continuous parameters are well established, the discrete and high-dimensional nature of treespace poses substantial challenges. In this paper, we introduce a new approach based on Conditional Clade Distributions (CCDs) to emulate MCMC chains with known ESS bounds. We compare existing tree ESS estimators with novel approaches that utilize CCDs as tractable tree distributions, as well as a new probabilistic estimator based on differences in clade frequencies between independent chains. Using our emulated chains from both simulated and real datasets, we assess estimators for their ability to recover the true ESS (accuracy), their insensitivity to the removal of autocorrelated samples from the chain (stability), and their tolerance to combining multiple chains together (robustness). We further examine how multimodality and poor inter-mode chain mixing can compromise the reliability of tree ESS estimates. These findings indicate that our new CCD-based estimators perform comparably to existing approaches with respect to accuracy, stability, and robustness. In contrast, the probabilistic estimator and two previously recommended methods incur prohibitive computational costs for long chains. Together, these results establish a new framework for evaluating tree ESS estimators using CCD-based emulated MCMC chains and demonstrate their performance and current limitations in practical phylogenetic analyses. The expanded suite of tree ESS estimators is available in the user-friendly TreeStat2 software package for BEAST 2.

items.title: Cultural evolution shaped human's uniquely sensitive disgust avoidance
items.summary: Disgust is an emotion that serves to avoid contaminants, and is central to the behavioural immune system. While disgust-motivated avoidance occurs in bonobos and chimpanzees, humans show uniquely high levels of contamination sensitivity. There is some disagreement over to what extent human disgust avoidance is a genetic adaptation or shaped through social transmission, and whether parental modelling plays a role in the latter. Here, we address this debate by simulating 100,000 years of cultural and biological evolution in various scenarios. We modelled disgust as a trait that governed the extent to which individuals forewent potentially contaminated nutrition. This lowered their risk of gastrointestinal illness, at the cost of increasing starvation risk and birth-interval. As environmental levels and costs of contamination rose, so did relative fitness of high disgust-avoidant individuals. Evolutionary shifts in disgust as polygenic trait occurred as a consequence of germ-cell mutations, but were most prominent in populations with high initial genetic variance. Crucially, cultural transmission between generations operated at a higher rate, even if parental modelling was eliminated. These results underscore the plausibility of cultural evolution's role in shaping human's uniquely sensitive disgust avoidance, and serves as an illustration of emerging theories that paint affective and cognitive mechanisms as socially transmitted rather than genetic adaptations.

items.title: Tensor-based Fusion of Multi-modal Data for Predicting Cancer Risk Levels
items.summary: Cancer diagnosis and treatment increasingly rely on multi-modal diagnostic technologies that generate high-dimensional datasets. Although these datasets are rich in pathological information, they pose considerable challenges in interpretation, dimensionality reduction, and clinical applicability. Conventional machine learning approaches often fail to extract meaningful cross-modal features, thereby limiting predictive accuracy in patient risk stratification. To address these limitations, this paper proposes an unsupervised machine learning framework that integrates feature extraction, tensor decomposition, and clustering to improve cancer risk prediction. The framework employs tensor decomposition to fuse heterogeneous genomic and clinical data, enabling the extraction of latent, biologically meaningful features that outperform unimodal feature sets. Multiple feature extraction strategies are investigated, and the resulting features are subsequently clustered using a range of clustering algorithms. Comparative evaluations based on internal and external metrics are then used to identify the most effective configurations. The framework is validated on LinkedOmics data comprising 11,158 patients across 32 cancer types. For patient risk stratification, clinically relevant attributes such as tumor purity, pathological stage, and survival outcomes serve as ground-truth indicators. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of tSVD+GMM, which consistently outperforms other configurations across clinical benchmarks.

items.title: Double-Take: Improving Capacity, Binding, and Selectivity In Long-Context Within Bidirectional Memory
items.summary: Processing a long sequence does not guarantee that distant information remains usable. As context grows, a fixed-size memory must retain many associations, connect information across positions, and preserve relevant structure without being overwhelmed by everything it observes. These are distinct requirements: a memory may store more information without representing the relationships needed for retrieval, and it may transport those relationships without preserving the ones that matter. Thus, the challenge is not simply extending context length, but constructing a memory that remains usable as context grows. We study this problem in large-chunk test-time training (TTT) and identify two basic failures: single-step writes accumulate interference, limiting capacity, while self-associative writes cannot form cross-position bindings. We introduce Double-Take (DT), which repairs these failures with multi-step unpinned updates and cross-position mixing, and adds bidirectional change-sensitive writes for selective retention. Capacity alone leaves end-to-end recall at the $0.10$ chance floor; adding binding raises it to $0.92$. Trained only on $32\,\mathrm{kb}$ genomic contexts, DT reaches $0.927$ AUROC at $131\,\mathrm{kb}$ and $0.856$ near $1\,\mathrm{Mb}$, while transferring zero-shot from human to mouse. Together, these results identify capacity, binding, and selectivity as three requirements for usable long-range memory.

items.title: FlyHack: Stress-Testing Mechanistic Claims in a Connectome-Constrained Visual Model
items.summary: Connectome-constrained neural networks make biological components directly accessible to intervention, but their mechanistic conclusions can still depend on the comparison model, intervention, circuit representation and trained solution. We stress-test these dependencies in flyvis, a \emph{Drosophila} motion-vision model, using its 50-model ensemble, task-matched causal CNN controls and replicated interventions. At the level of model behaviour, three-level reverse-phi reversal in flyvis is strongly period- and velocity-dependent and also appears in task-matched CNNs; neither family reproduces the fly's stationary-sawtooth response. Adversarial direction reversal requires a perturbation bound of 0.21--0.27 times stimulus contrast in flyvis versus 0.13--0.25 in CNNs, but the gap over a parameter-matched CNN largely closes for larger CNNs. At the level of mechanism, matching attribution to the intervention matters: for held-out-mean replacement, first-order edge attribution patching reaches pooled AUROC 0.970 and Spearman 0.872, versus 0.933 and 0.126 when its zero-aligned score is evaluated against the same ground truth. Circuit conclusions also vary with representation and ensemble member. Greedy cell-type sets meet a model-relative T4/T5 tuning criterion in 25 of 50 models, while T4/T5 output silencing reduces the tested optic-flow behaviour to at most two of eight clips in 40. In six models where the cell-type search first succeeds, the corresponding connection sets can be pruned to 13--31 added classes; under an additional two-sided response-amplitude check, only two of those six first-success cell-type sets still meet the tuning threshold. These results support a narrower use of connectome-constrained models: they make mechanistic hypotheses directly testable, but the resulting claims must be scoped to the model family, intervention, representation and trained solution.

items.title: TopoLIA: Topology-Inspired Latent Interaction Attention for Drug Discovery
items.summary: The growing sophistication of drug discovery calls for new advances in artificial intelligence (AI). Transformers have underpinned recent breakthroughs in AI, yet their conventional source-target attention mechanism can become a bottleneck for modeling complex interactions. Here, we introduce TopoLIA, a topology-inspired latent interaction attention mechanism that learns not only how much information should be exchanged between interaction partners, but also how that information should be transformed. Source-target-dependent attention is mediated through a compact latent interaction space, providing a structured representation of complex interactions. We further incorporate topological spectral representations to capture multiscale data geometry and extract algebraic relationships. TopoLIA thus incorporates topological principles into both data representation and neural network architecture. We demonstrate TopoLIA on protein-ligand binding, where persistent spectra encode multiscale topological and geometric patterns in 3D protein-ligand complexes, while latent interaction attention (LIA) enables structured, source-target-dependent information exchange. We pretrain TopoLIA by reconstructing masked multiscale spectral tokens from unlabeled molecular structures, yielding transferable structural representations without task-specific annotations. Across multiple scoring and docking benchmarks, TopoLIA achieves state-of-the-art performance and consistently outperforms its standard-attention counterpart. Rank analyses show that compact latent dimensions yield the best performance, supporting compact interaction spaces as an effective inductive bias for biomolecular learning. More broadly, LIA provides a general framework for structured, source-target-dependent information exchange that is applicable to diverse scientific and AI problems involving complex heterogeneous interactions.

items.title: Organisms Write Their Own Evolution: Direct Epigenomic Inheritance Accelerates Learning on Compositional Tasks
items.summary: What if organisms could write their own evolution? For 150 years, evolution has been understood as one-way: genes provide the rules, organisms respond to selection. But if organisms could learn during their lifetime, write that learned knowledge directly into their epigenome -- the heritable regulatory layer controlling gene expression -- and pass it to offspring, then knowledge would accumulate across generations instead of being rediscovered by each one. Such direct epigenomic inheritance would constitute genuine organismal agency: writing new information into heredity rather than passively receiving it. To test whether organisms actually benefit from this capability, we implement Phenopoiesis, a computational model in which organisms maintain two independent heritable layers: a genetic layer (inherited with mutation) and an epigenetic layer (inherited unchanged). We compare Phenopoiesis against Selection Only (no learning) and the Baldwin Effect (learning influences selection but is not inherited) across six learning tasks of increasing complexity: three simple (learn one pattern) and three compositional (learn two patterns simultaneously). On simple tasks all three mechanisms perform equivalently (p = 0.559): complexity is required for inheritance to matter. On learnable compositional tasks, Phenopoiesis outperforms the alternatives by 3-6x in fitness (F = 177-358, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 3.44-4.89), with perfect reproducibility (s.d. = 0.0 on T+Plus across all 30 runs), indicating deterministic knowledge accumulation: offspring inherit their parents' learned solutions and add new learning on top. On a geometrically incompatible task all mechanisms fail equally, revealing an inherent limit. These results give the first direct computational test of Denis Noble's hypothesis that organisms possess read-write access to their own heredity, and show precisely when that access pays off.

items.title: Coupling with opinion dynamics promotes prosocial behavior in multilayer networks
items.summary: Various theoretical and empirical studies have accounted for why humans cooperate in competitive environments. Although prior work has revealed that network structure and multiplex interactions can promote cooperation, most theory assumes that individuals play dilemma games in all social contexts. However, real-world agents may participate in a diversity of interactions, not all of which present dilemmas. We develop an evolutionary game model on multilayer networks in which one layer supports the prisoner's dilemma game, while the other follows constant-selection dynamics, representing biased but non-dilemmatic competition, akin to opinion or fad spreading. Our theoretical analysis reveals that coupling a social dilemma layer to a non-dilemmatic constant-selection layer robustly enhances cooperation in many cases, across different multilayer networks, updating rules, and payoff schemes. These findings suggest that embedding individuals within diverse networked settings---even those unrelated to direct social dilemmas---can be a principled approach to engineering cooperation in socio-ecological and organizational systems.

items.title: Bayesian Sampling of Structural Ensembles: The Role of Ensemble-Counting Measures
items.summary: Structural ensemble refinement is widely used to integrate molecular simulations with experimental measurements. While most applications focus on the maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) ensemble, Bayesian sampling of the posterior distribution can provide uncertainty estimates and posterior averages for arbitrary observables. A notable step in this direction was introduced by the Bayesian Energy Landscape Tilting (BELT) framework, where sampling is performed on a family of maximum-entropy ensembles parametrized by Lagrange multipliers. Here, we show that Bayesian sampling in this setting requires an explicit choice of ensemble-counting measure. In particular, the flat measure in Lagrange-multiplier space used in the original BELT formulation leads to a posterior distribution that is formally non-normalizable for finite reference trajectories. We propose the Jeffreys measure as an invariant ensemble-counting prescription, restoring normalizability in the finite-sample situations considered here, and providing a consistent definition of posterior averages. Using both an analytically tractable Gaussian model and maximum-entropy refinement of RNA oligomer simulations, we compare different ensemble-counting measures and show that they can significantly affect Bayesian estimates. The resulting methodology has been implemented in the \texttt{MDRefine} software package.

items.title: Energy, Information, and the Limits of Neuropsychiatric Classification
items.summary: Importance: The search for reliable neuroimaging biomarkers of mental disorders has remained elusive despite decades of research. Why clinically consequential disorders yield weak neuroimaging separability remains unresolved. Drawing on statistical thermodynamics and the metabolic costs of neural coding, we propose that psychiatric disorders produce constrained deformations of a largely shared repertoire of brain activity patterns, limiting the class-specific information available for classification. Observations: We develop a framework linking physical resource constraints, landscape deformation, distributional separation, and attainable classification, and examine its components using human neuroimaging, synthetic data, and an exactly specified physical model. In resting-state fMRI from 1952 FOR2107 participants (823 with major depressive disorder; 1129 healthy controls), held-out energy-landscape estimates and nonlinear classifiers agreed across 13 comparisons (r = 0.996). Similar results emerged at both FOR2107 centers and in 900 SRPBS participants spanning multiple psychiatric diagnoses. In synthetic data, classification improved with distributional separation and approached the optimum. In an equilibrium three-well model, statistical energy equaled physical potential energy scaled by inverse temperature. Modest deformation redistributed state occupancy while optimal snapshot classification remained weak. A literature map found insufficiently comparable evidence to test the human metabolic constraint. Conclusions: Clinically consequential differences may arise within a largely shared neural repertoire. The thermodynamic framework connects physical deformation to classification under specified assumptions; its metabolic implementation in humans remains untested. Testing this mechanism requires joint measurements of brain activity, bodily physiology, and metabolism.

items.title: Parameter Identifiability beyond the Fisher Information Approximation in Data-Driven Modeling
items.summary: Data-driven mechanistic modeling of high-dimensional biological data requires rigorous parameter identifiability. Profile likelihood entails costly repeated optimization, while Fisher-information criteria discard the model's Hessian and may misjudge weakly constrained directions. From a well-posedness definition of identifiability we characterize the stability of the estimated parameters under data perturbations while retaining the full Hessian. It yields Hölder-$\tfrac12$ stability for a zero residual when the Fisher information is degenerate and corrects the Fisher matrix otherwise; residual and perturbation sizes decide the order of stability, Lipschitz below a crossover scale proportional to the residual norm and Hölder-$\tfrac12$ above. In a local quadratic approximation we derive coordinate identifiability metrics allowing singular Jacobians and nuisance Hessian blocks, and spectral bounds link the corrections to parameter and prediction uncertainty. Applications to JAK--STAT signaling, HIV dynamics, and amyloid-$β$ accumulation support the theory. Requiring only local derivatives, the framework offers a tractable basis for identifiability analysis of large-scale models.

items.title: Lyapunov spectrum of random neural networks
items.summary: The Lyapunov spectrum of a nonlinear recurrent neural network with random asymmetric couplings is calculated in the limit $N\to\infty$. The calculation is based on a finite-$N$ identity that expresses the cumulative distribution of Lyapunov exponents as a response function of the tangent-space dynamics, with the tangent trajectory selected by a minimum-norm condition rather than by an initial condition. A cavity method then determines this response function at large $N$ through a self-consistent single-site problem. This result establishes that the chaos in this network is extensive and gives access to diffeomorphism-invariant properties of the dynamics. This work was done in collaboration with the AI models GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5.

items.title: A minimal model for rate-induced tipping to extinction
items.summary: Rate-induced tipping ("R-tipping") in ecological modelling is characterised by too-rapid change of an environmental parameter causing collapse of a population without any bifurcation being crossed ("B-tipping"). A well-known example of a slow-fast predator-prey model in which R-tipping is observed [Vanselow, Wieczorek, Feudel, Journal of Theoretical Biology, 479, 64-72 (2019)] suffers from unecological "resurgence", whereby populations driven to functional extinction recover towards stable coexistence. We propose an analytically tractable model, incorporating a strong Allee effect into the prey dynamics in a slow-fast Lotka-Volterra-type predator-prey system, which induces bistability and thus renders the extinction state a genuine attractor. Applying geometric singular perturbation theory (GSPT), we describe the dynamics of the extended model that is obtained by "ramping" of the inverse prey carrying capacity. We show the presence of a parabolic-shaped, folded critical manifold which admits a folded saddle singularity, the strong canard of which separates solutions that track the moving coexistence state from those that tip to extinction. The analytical simplicity of our model allows us to derive explicit expressions for the critical rate that separates "tracking" from "tipping" dynamics. Finally, we argue that our system represents a minimal model for rate-induced tipping to extinction, in that it incorporates three essential ingredients: bistability, a folded critical manifold, and a folded-saddle-type canard.

items.title: Unlocking the Regulatory Genome by ARGUS: An Evidence-Constrained Agentic Framework for Interpreting Single Nucleotide Variants
items.summary: Over 90% of disease-associated variants from genome-wide association studies fall in noncoding regulatory regions, yet their functional interpretation remains a central open problem in genomic medicine. Large language models prompted to interpret such variants routinely hallucinate transcription factor (TF) binding changes, fabricate experimental support, and assign biological significance to statistically negligible signals. We present ARGUS (Agentic Regulatory Genomics for an Uncertainty-aware Scientist), which strictly separates deterministic biological computation from LLM-mediated reasoning. ARGUS wraps 458 DNABERT-based TF binding models in a hypothesis-directed investigation loop where a planner selects evidence sources based on current uncertainty, a verifier deterministically interprets each observation, and intermediate results change the investigation path. On variant rs6983267 at the 8q24 cancer risk locus, the same planner produces four divergent trajectories for four TFs. FOXA1 is rescued in 3 steps when real ADASTRA allele-specific binding data (15 experiments, FDR = 0.030) reveals a model false negative masked by saturation. KLF6 traverses 8 steps across ADASTRA, JASPAR motif analysis, and ENCODE cCRE regulatory annotation before abstaining due to mixed indirect evidence. RAD21 abstains in 8 steps after ADASTRA returns a coverage-qualified but nonsignificant allelic test (5 experiments, FDR = 0.65), and SP1, which shares FOXA1's saturated retained prediction, abstains because no direct experimental evidence exists at this locus. All observations come from real ADASTRA, JASPAR, and ENCODE cCRE queries; none are simulated. A comparison of fixed-priority and LLM-mediated planning shows that the LLM planner reaches identical verdicts with fewer tool calls by declining evidence that cannot resolve the claim under test.

items.title: La-Ribo: RNA Co-Design via Geometry-Latent Flow Matching
items.summary: RNA function arises from the coupling of nucleotide sequence and three-dimensional structure, motivating their joint design. Coordinating global folding with nucleotide-level detail remains challenging under limited structural supervision. We introduce La-Ribo, a generative framework for RNA sequence-structure co-design via geometry-latent flow matching. La-Ribo retains a sparse phosphate-sugar--base scaffold and encodes nucleotide identity and local conformation in residue-wise latents. A shared flow network generates both jointly, and an RNA-specific decoder then reconstructs all heavy atoms. To expand supervision, we construct a quality-controlled corpus of 168,561 RNA structures, integrating experimental data with predictions from three folding models, including 10,631 MSA-supported structures generated in this work. La-Ribo improves designability and codesignability over the evaluated baselines across sampling budgets and two refolding models, and the same prior supports scaffold-conditioned inverse folding without additional training.

items.title: CMGL: Confidence-guided Multi-omics Graph Learning for Cancer Subtype Classification
items.summary: Motivation: Multi-omics integration can improve cancer subtyping, but modality informativeness and noise vary across cancer types and patients. Most graph methods for multi-omics data learn modality contributions within the downstream classification objective, leaving predictive reliability for each patient implicit. As a result, uninformative modalities can weaken the fused representation, while unreliable omics can introduce noisy patient relationships into graph propagation. To address these two problems, we propose CMGL, which produces a separate reliability estimate before fusion and uses consensus patient neighborhoods for graph classification. Results: CMGL estimates modality confidence for each patient through evidential deep learning, fixes these values during fusion across omics, and performs classification on an independently specified consistency graph. On four MLOmics cancer-subtype tasks and the 32-class pan-cancer task, CMGL consistently improves over the strongest baseline, surpassing it by 4.03% in average accuracy on the four single-cancer tasks. Its representations recover the PAM50 intrinsic subtypes of breast invasive carcinoma (BRCA), and the model trained on BRCA transfers without fine tuning to kidney renal clear cell carcinoma (KIRC), stratifying patients into prognostically distinct groups.

items.title: Beta frequency shifts in decision making: Spectral fingerprints or communication channels?
items.summary: Recent evidence suggests that beta-band activity plays a key role in decision-making. Here we review our recent work in humans and non-human primates showing that beta-band frequency shifts in frontal cortex signal categorical decision outcomes. We revisit our previous proposal suggesting that content-specific beta reflects the flexible recruiting of transient neural ensembles and update it to emphasize frequency as the relevant parameter. We argue that beta frequency shifts arise from changes in connectivity between weakly coupled oscillators and that, more than a spectral fingerprint, they reflect an active mechanism to (re)-activate behaviorally relevant communication channels in the brain.

items.title: Neural Decoding as Cognitive Inference
items.summary: The brain maintains stable cognition despite continuously changing neural activity. How to extract stable cognitive states from variable neural observations remains a central problem in neural decoding. Existing neural decoding methods map neural observations to predefined external labels based on the stimulus-response principle, often capturing recording-specific spurious correlations. Inspired by how the brain infers the world, and specifically by Bayesian brain theory, we recast neural decoding as cognitive inference constrained by brain-intrinsic priors, yielding high-level meta-neural semantic representations. In decoding experiments spanning five neural recording modalities and three cognitive domains (motor, perception and internal mentation), our cognitive inference method reorganized the geometry of neural observation representations, yielding meta-neural semantic representations that exhibited consistent geometric relationships across cognitive tasks and enabled the recovery of stable cognitive states from variable neural observations. Our work provides an account of how the brain maintains relatively stable cognition despite continual changes in the external environment. Cognitive stability is sustained through cognitive inference from changing neural activity, without requiring fixed neural activity patterns.

items.title: Three-dimensional imaging of isolated membrane-protein complexes in vacuo with an X-ray laser
items.summary: The prospect of imaging single biomolecules, viruses and cells with intense, ultrashort X-ray pulses has driven the development of X-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs). However, the weak scattering from small particles is easily swamped by background from residual gas, which has so far limited applications to strongly scattering targets such as viruses, cell organelles and cells. Here we report a three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction of an isolated 1-MDa membrane-protein complex, photosystem I (PS I), from single-particle diffraction data. PS I trimers were aerosolised by charge-reduction electrospray ionisation and injected into the European XFEL beam, with partial helium gas exchange reducing background scattering by 80%. From 32 788 diffraction patterns of single trimers in random orientations, we reconstructed the 3D electron density to a resolution of 3.8 nm, limited by the detector geometry. The disc-shaped density, about 22 nm across and 10 nm thick, matches the size of a PS I trimer in a detergent micelle and is consistent with the compaction predicted by molecular dynamics simulations of the complex in vacuo and observed in native mass spectrometry. These results show that membrane-protein complexes can be imaged in vacuo with X-ray lasers, an important step towards ultrafast diffractive imaging of single macromolecules.

items.title: Elucidating the Space of Enzymatic Reaction: A Unified Benchmark and Pretrained Model
items.summary: Existing reaction models primarily learn molecular transformations, whereas enzy- matic reactions depend jointly on molecular structure and catalytic function. We formulate this problem as learning an enzymatic reaction space linking reactants, products, and Enzyme Commission (EC) annotations. To characterize this space, we introduce VenusRX-Bench, a unified benchmark for forward reaction prediction, single-step retrosynthesis, and EC-number prediction. VenusRX-Bench integrates reactions from multiple biochemical databases with standardized curation, leakage- controlled splits, and consistent evaluation. Benchmarking representative chemical and enzymatic models reveals a clear chemical-to-enzymatic domain gap, driven by limited domain data, catalytic-context dependency, and the difficulty of modeling large biomolecular structures. To bridge this gap, we develop VenusRX, a unified T5-style sequence-to-sequence model for enzymatic reactions. VenusRX jointly learns forward prediction, ret- rosynthesis, and reaction reconstruction, with two-stage training on millions of template-expanded reactions followed by real biochemical reactions. In addition, optional EC conditioning incorporates catalytic context, while Molecule Library- Constrained Decoding improves the generation of complex biomolecules. Across benchmark tasks and challenging generalization splits, VenusRX achieves the best or competitive performance on most evaluated settings over representative chem- ical and enzymatic baselines. Moreover, EC information consistently improves reaction prediction, while learned reaction representations support accurate EC prediction, revealing a bidirectional relationship between reaction structure and catalytic function. Together, VenusRX-Bench and VenusRX provide a unified framework for elucidating and modeling enzymatic reaction space

items.title: Persistence of bounded trajectories in positively transverse reaction networks
items.summary: We introduce positively transverse reaction networks and show that, with mass-action kinetics, no bounded trajectory with positive initial condition has a boundary omega-limit point. These networks are characterized by a geometric property of a collection of polytopes defined by a subset of complexes of the network.

items.title: Certified Scalable Enclosures for Uncertain Underdetermined Systems
items.summary: The central challenge in underdetermined models with bounded uncertainty, such as in nonlinear design and estimation, is certifying the solution sets. Conventional solution methodologies, such as those based on Newton's method or on sampling-based uncertainty quantification, are either not applicable due to the underdetermined nature or do not give guarantees that all solutions have been found, assuming they converge. We addressed this issue for a problem that arises in nonlinear design, where a target steady-state box is prescribed and the parameters have to be found. We developed a trapezoidal linearisation method that rigorously encloses all solutions and combined it with a tractable linear programming method to compute the component-wise bounds. We showed that the resulting families of linear programs can iteratively contract an initial parameter region. A subdivision of the target state and the initial parameter region can improve the contraction and provide tighter enclosures. The trapezoidal relaxation gives a family of linear programs that can also be used for finding solutions for interval linear systems via the Oettli-Prager characterisation. We demonstrate the generality of the method through different applications, including nonlinear design in biomolecular circuits, a sensitivity analysis method, and in a compressed sensing context, and discuss the trade-off between enclosure tightness and computational cost.

items.title: Beyond Action Entropy: Quotient-Space Exploration for Genome-Scale Metabolic Model Repair
items.summary: Repairing scientific models from functional observations differs fundamentally from supervised prediction: feedback may certify a solution without revealing which structural correction is responsible. We study this setting for genome-scale metabolic model (GEM) repair, where multiple reaction edits can explain the same phenotypes and many apparently distinct edits correspond to the same biological mechanism. This many-to-one structure creates a hidden failure mode for conventional exploration: diversity in the output space need not translate into diversity of scientific hypotheses. We introduce QuotientPO, which collapses equivalent repairs into canonical mechanisms and optimizes exploration directly over the resulting quotient space. To make quotient exploration informative under finite rollouts, we derive a kernelized Rényi estimator that resolves graded crowding among distinct repair cores beyond coarse exact-match counts. On 2,212 held-out GEMs, QuotientPO improves Success@32 from 17.93% to 20.10% (+12.1% relative) while consistently increasing distinct successful-core discovery under the same sampling budget. These results establish quotient-space exploration as a principled approach to mechanism-level discovery under verifier-induced equivalence.

items.title: Leveraging secondary-structure information for accurate nucleic acid structure prediction with OFoldNA
items.summary: Recent advances in biomolecular structure prediction have enabled accurate modelling of increasingly complex molecular systems. However, nucleic acid structure prediction remains challenging because of conformational flexibility and the limited availability of high-quality 3D structural data.
