Since locational pricing can introduce price unfairness when grid constraints are active, the proposed approach includes mechanisms to enforce price fairness across the network. The method involves the DSO solving a scenario-based optimal power flow (OPF) problem to derive, similarly to locational marginal prices in transmission systems, the Lagrange multipliers associated with grid constraints and to compute individualized price signals for each prosumer under various PV generation and demand scenarios. Subsequently, two methods are introduced to aggregate these individualized prices into a single fair price across prosumers. Their performance is evaluated through simulations on a model distribution grid, comparing prosumer revenues, grid constraint violations, and analyzing the impact of fairness on reducing cost variance among prosumers.

items.title: Uncertainty Quantification and Risk Control for Multiple Sound Source Localization
items.summary: Reliable Sound Source Localization (SSL) plays an essential role in many downstream tasks, where informed decision making depends not only on accurate localization but also on the confidence in each estimate. This need for reliability becomes even more pronounced in challenging conditions, such as reverberant environments and multi-source scenarios. However, existing SSL methods typically provide only point estimates, offering limited or no Uncertainty Quantification (UQ). We leverage the Conformal Prediction (CP) framework and its extensions for controlling general risk functions to develop two complementary UQ approaches for SSL. The first assumes that the number of active sources is known and constructs prediction regions that cover the true source locations. The second addresses the more challenging setting where the source count is unknown, first reliably estimating the number of active sources and then forming corresponding prediction regions. We evaluate the proposed methods on extensive simulations and real-world recordings across varying reverberation levels and source configurations. Results demonstrate reliable finite-sample guarantees and consistent performance for both known and unknown source-count scenarios, highlighting the practical utility of the proposed frameworks for uncertainty-aware SSL.

items.title: Adaptive Handling of Deadline Misses via Stochastic MPC
items.summary: Real-time control systems may experience sporadic computational overloads that cause controller executions to overrun their expected deadlines, affecting the timely update of control inputs. Such overruns are classically handled with static decisions, e.g., by either stopping and discarding the late execution at the deadline instant, or continuing it while skipping the next activations. This paper first demonstrates that such static policies can lead to suboptimal performance when the controlled system undergoes varying operating conditions, and thus proposes a control-driven hybrid overrun strategy that optimally adapts the deadline miss handling at runtime. We model the closed loop as a Markov jump linear system, whose modes encode overrun histories, and we formulate a scenario-tree-based stochastic model predictive control problem that predicts and optimizes over possible sequences of deadline hits and misses. We evaluate our proposal on linear benchmarks including a double integrator and an aircraft pitch system.

items.title: Time-Varying Parametric Channel Estimation With CP Decomposition Tensor Processing
items.summary: Integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) is a key use case for sixth-generation (6G) wireless systems, where parametric channel estimation (PCE) plays a central role in enabling sensing, localization, and channel equalization in high-mobility scenarios. However, PCE is typically more computationally demanding than conventional channel estimation, which motivates the development of lower-complexity solutions. In this letter, we propose a fast PCE algorithm for time-varying and frequency-selective (TVFS) channels based on canonical polyadic (CP) decomposition and tensor processing, combined with ESPRIT-based initialization, component refinement, and exact line-search alternating coordinate descent. Two variants are presented: one for fully digital and another for hybrid receiver architectures. Numerical results show that the proposed method clearly outperforms a related CP-based baseline while achieving estimation performance close to a multiple-start SAGE benchmark at a substantially lower computational cost, with about one order of magnitude shorter execution time.

items.title: Infrastructure-Aware Runtime Protection of Co-Deployed AI Services at the Industrial Edge
items.summary: In modern production lines, a single edge device simultaneously runs multiple AI services like a torque-control model, a vision inspector, a predictive maintenance routine. All these services run on the same CPU and same shared network segment. When the shared network segment saturates, the services do not crash. The services just produce outputs that are inaccurate or stale, and no longer reflect the plant's conditions. Our paper targets this class of silent, partial failure scenarios in Industrial Edge Systems. We treat each co-deployed service as an autonomous agent. We introduce the Runtime Criticality Score (RCS), which each service agent uses to express at any moment, its intrinsic utility and survival urgency under resource constraints. The score is computed from six normalized dimensions covering physical consequence, inference quality, input freshness, recent availability stress, actuator coupling, and available protective actions on the host. Its dimension weights are adjusted online through a lightweight Bayesian update driven by the type of disturbance currently observed, so the same service is ranked differently under a network delay than under thermal throttling. Agents publish their RCS to peers over an open, peer-to-peer discovery channel, and use it to negotiate three things without a central controller: (i) local threshold enforcement on their own host, (ii) migration to a willing peer when the current host can no longer protect them, (iii) reassignment of the coordination role when the incumbent coordinator is itself impaired. Beyond the immediate benefit of catching silent degradation, the framework contributes a concrete instance of decentralized, physically grounded agent coordination. Agents belonging to different owners can advertise capabilities, bid for protection, and reorganize across an open network.

items.title: Lyapunov characterization of boundedness of reachability sets for infinite-dimensional systems
items.summary: We prove a converse Lyapunov theorem for boundedness of reachability sets for a general class of control systems whose flow is Lipschitz continuous on compact intervals with respect to trajectory-dominated inputs. We show that this condition is satisfied by broad classes of semilinear evolution equations. For ordinary differential equations, as a consequence of our results, we obtain a converse Lyapunov theorem for forward completeness, without a priori restrictions on the magnitude of inputs. As an example, we rederive Wintner's classical result using our Lyapunov approach.

items.title: BALLAST: Physics-Aware Moving Target Defense for Industrial Control Systems Using a Digital Twin Safety Oracle
items.summary: Industrial Control Systems run on static network configurations, which leaves an attacker unlimited time to map the plant. Moving Target Defense answers this by shuffling addresses, but almost every published scheme never checks whether the reconfiguration will itself disturb the physical process it protects, so the defense can destabilise a control loop or trip an actuator. We present BALLAST, which places a learned Digital Twin between the security policy and the plant as a safety oracle. A physics-informed LSTM surrogate forecasts the physical effect of a candidate network change, a reinforcement learning agent trades security entropy against process stability, and a connection-draining handover lets in-flight Modbus transactions complete before the old mapping is withdrawn. An explicit shield rejects any action whose predicted trajectory would leave the safe operating envelope. On the SWaT water treatment testbed, Ballast cut the success rate of an adversary's reconnaissance sweep by 85 percent and recorded no safety violation across 50 runs, a 95 percent upper bound of 5.8 percent on the violation rate, against five violations and a tracking error 19 times larger for RL-MTD, the closest published analogue to our design. Measured against the strongest baseline on the physical metrics, a threshold-triggered scheme that itself records one violation rather than RL-MTD's five, Ballast still improves the tracking error by a factor of 2.5 and removes that remaining violation. The gain costs a small and deliberate concession in raw deterrence. Twin inference meets the 50 ms budget on a workstation core and an embedded GPU, and is projected to meet it on both edge CPUs when the three envelope stages are evaluated in a single batched call; the complete decision-to-enforcement path was measured only on the workstation.

items.title: A Ray-Based Characterization of Satellite-to-Urban Propagation
items.summary: The evolution toward 6G communication systems is expected to rely on integrated three-dimensional network architectures where terrestrial infrastructures coexist with non-terrestrial stations such as satellites, enabling ubiquitous connectivity and service continuity. In this context, accurate channel models for satellite-to-ground propagation in urban environments are essential, particularly for user equipment located at street level where obstruction and multipath effects are significant. This work investigates satellite-to-urban propagation through deterministic ray-tracing simulations. Three representative urban layouts are considered, namely dense urban, urban, and suburban. Multiple use cases are investigated, including handheld devices, vehicular terminals, and fixed rooftop receivers operating across several frequency bands. The analysis focuses on the relative importance of competing propagation mechanisms and on four key channel parameters, namely shadowing standard deviation, Rician \(K\)-factor, delay spread and Doppler spread, which are relevant for the calibration of channel models to be used in link- and system-level simulations. Results show that elevation and receiver placement strongly shape fading and dispersion, antenna directivity affects shadowing differently under LoS and NLoS conditions, urban morphology produces nontrivial multipath trends, and terminal mobility largely governs Doppler spread.

items.title: UEPS: Robust and Efficient MRI Reconstruction
items.summary: Deep unrolled models (DUM) have become the state-of-the-art for accelerated MRI reconstruction, yet their robustness under domain shift remains a critical barrier to clinical adoption. In this work, we identify coil sensitivity map (CSM) estimation as the primary bottleneck limiting generalization. To address this, we propose UEPS, a novel DUM architecture featuring three key designs: (i) an Unrolled Expanded (UE) design that eliminates CSM dependency by reconstructing each coil independently; (ii) progressive resolution, which leverages k-space-to-image mapping for efficient coarse-to-fine refinement; and (iii) sparse attention tailored to MRI's 1D undersampling nature. These physics-grounded designs enable gains in robustness and computational efficiency. We construct a large-scale zero-shot transfer benchmark comprising 10 out-of-distribution (OOD) test sets spanning diverse clinical shifts, anatomy, view, contrast, vendor, field strength, and coil configurations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UEPS consistently and substantially outperforms existing DUM, end-to-end, diffusion, and untrained methods across all OOD tests, achieving state-of-the-art robustness with low-latency inference suitable for real-time deployment.

items.title: On Over-Conservatism Under Low-Probability Extreme Events: A KL-Regularized Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Planning Method
items.summary: The increasing penetration of renewable energy makes power systems more vulnerable to low-probability extreme events, elevating system planning to a critical role in ensuring reliability. Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) based on the Wasserstein distance is widely used to address this challenge. However, we find that the conventional Wasserstein ambiguity set tends to excessively amplify the probabilities of low-probability extreme events, leading to over-conservative investment decisions. To mitigate this over-conservatism, this paper proposes a novel ambiguity set that modifies the Wasserstein distance with a Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence regularization term. By leveraging the KL divergence's sensitivity to relative probability changes, the proposed set effectively curbs the unrealistic magnification of low-probability events. A two-stage distributionally robust planning model built upon this new ambiguity set is developed to optimize the installed capacity of photovoltaic, wind, and energy storage. The complex model is then reformulated as an equivalent exponential cone program with strict theoretical proofs, making it computationally tractable. Numerical results on the PJM 5-bus and IEEE 118-bus systems reveal the over-conservatism of standard Wasserstein DRO under low-probability extreme events and validate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed planning model and solution algorithm.

items.title: PING: physics informed graph neural network for advection-diffusion processes with applications to solar power forecasting
items.summary: Advection-diffusion plays an essential role in transport phenomena such as atmospheric and cloud dynamics. Improved forecasting of cloud motion, in turn, enhances solar power production forecasts and facilitates the integration of additional photovoltaic (PV) sources into the power grid. However, both classical numerical models and emerging deep learning approaches face challenges when applied to spatially irregular sensor networks such as those formed by weather stations. In this work, we adopt a graph signal processing perspective and model advection-diffusion particles as signals on a graph to capture the dynamics of these processes. We introduce a Physics-Informed Graph Neural Network (PING) for forecasting future advection-diffusion particle concentrations on irregular grids. The model incorporates a discretized advection-diffusion equation as a soft constraint in the loss function to guide learning toward physically consistent solutions. This model is on par with state of the art models on synthetic and real transport phenomena datasets, including sea surface temperature and cloud index datasets. Furthermore, the PING model is successfully coupled with models for forecasting PV power production. This hybrid approach leverages data fusion from ground-based sensors at PV stations and satellite images with cloud concentration to improve the accuracy of intra-day PV power production.

items.title: Convexity Meets Curvature: Lifted Near-Field Super-Resolution
items.summary: Extra-large apertures, high carrier frequencies, and integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) are pushing array processing into the Fresnel region, where spherical wavefronts induce a range-dependent phase across the aperture. This curvature breaks the Fourier/Vandermonde structure behind classical subspace methods, and it is especially limiting with hybrid front-ends that provide only a small number of pilot measurements. Consequently, practical systems need continuous angle resolution and joint angle-range inference where many near-field approaches still rely on costly 2D gridding. We show that convexity can meet curvature via a lifted, gridless superresolution framework for near-field measurements. The key is a Bessel-Vandermonde factorization of the Fresnel-phase manifold that exposes a hidden Vandermonde structure in angle while isolating the range dependence into a compact coefficient map. Building on this, we introduce a lifting that maps each range bin and continuous angle to a structured rank-one atom, converting the nonlinear near-field model into a linear inverse problem over a row-sparse matrix. Recovery is posed as atomic-norm minimization and an explicit dual characterization via bounded trigonometric polynomials yields certificate-based localization that super-resolves off-grid angles and identifies active range bins. Simulations with strongly undersampled hybrid observations validate reliable joint angle-range recovery for next-generation wireless and ISAC systems.

items.title: Fast Analytical Method for Resource Adequacy Assessment in Renewable-Rich Power Systems
items.summary: This paper proposes a novel analytical method for resource adequacy assessment in renewable rich power systems. The approach begins by applying the stress strength method to estimate two key resource adequacy indices: loss of load expectation (LOLE) and expected energy not supplied (EENS). This method requires defining the probability distribution functions (PDFs) for both the generation side and the load side. The load is assumed to follow a normal probability distribution, while the generation side probability distribution is derived from the combined PDFs of conventional, wind, and solar power sources. The approach models the cumulative impact of uncertainties on resource adequacy using the central limit theorem (CLT), and improves accuracy with a cumulant based Gram Charlier expansion when the CLT alone is insufficient. The effectiveness of the proposed method is validated through Monte Carlo simulations conducted on the IEEE single area and multi-area RTS-96 test systems. The results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a substantial reduction in computational time, which is crucial in the context of operational planning, without sacrificing accuracy. Furthermore, its performance improves as renewable penetration increases, making it particularly suitable for future power systems operation and planning.

items.title: Data-Driven Surrogate-Model for Real-Time Loads Prediction in Floating Wind Farms
items.summary: This work presents a data-driven load-surrogate modelling framework for real-time control of floating offshore wind farms. The proposed methodology uses mid-fidelity simulations performed with OpenFAST and FAST.Farm together with MLife fatigue analysis to generate Damage Equivalent Load (DEL) datasets of floating wind turbines under wake steering conditions. A two-stage surrogate modelling approach is adopted: first, a Feed-Forward Neural Network (FFNN) is trained using data from simulations of a single floating wind turbine, while a second stage corrects the residual error between the FFNN predictions and FAST.Farm simulations using either Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) or an additional FFNN. The results show that the proposed framework can estimate DELs with errors generally below 15% for tower base bending moment, blade root bending moment, yaw bearing moment, and fairlead tension, while maintaining computational times compatible with real-time applications. The study also highlights the challenges related to generalization of the load-surrogate model under varying environmental and control conditions, especially for large floating wind farms. Overall, the proposed methodology demonstrates the potential of surrogate-based DEL estimation for load-aware floating wind farm control applications.

items.title: FALLNEST: Dual-Domain Dataset Condensation of Imbalanced IMU Data for Wearable Fall Detection
items.summary: Wearable fall detection is hampered by rare fall events, scarce labeled IMU data, and the cost of training deep models on large, imbalanced corpora. Existing methods either rely on hand-crafted features with shallow classifiers, which limits learning from raw signals, or train deep networks on full datasets that require re-sampling to counter class skew and demand substantial data and compute. To address this, we propose a novel Fall detection framework via Normalized-gradient and Embedding matched Synthetic Time-frequency condensation, dubbed FALLNEST, a data-centric approach that distills large, imbalanced IMU datasets into tiny, class-balanced synthetic training sets. Building on dual-domain time-series condensation (CondTSC), FALLNEST introduces a fall-specific 7-channel input with accelerometer vector magnitude, class-balanced K-Means initialization, and normalized gradient matching with gradient clipping, combined with MMD-based embedding alignment and multi-view Fourier-domain augmentation, so that class balance arises from the condensed set itself rather than from re-sampling. We evaluate on SisFall, KFall, and MobiFall using strict subject-wise splits and naturally imbalanced test sets, reporting accuracy, Macro-F1, and PR-AUC over five seeds. A 102K-parameter TinyCNN trained on only 32 to 146 synthetic windows (about only 1% of the training windows) reaches 93.5-95.8% mean accuracy and 0.89-0.98 PR-AUC, with standard deviations of 1.0-1.7% in accuracy, demonstrating the efficacy of our approach.

items.title: Living Off the Grid: Continuous Range-Angle Super-Resolution for Near-Field XL-MIMO
items.summary: Near-field extremely large multiple input multiple output (XL-MIMO) breaks the assumptions that make classical super-resolution effective: the receiver acquires only a limited set of compressed pilot observations, while each propagation path is jointly determined by angle and distance under a spherical-wave model. This invalidates the far-field Vandermonde structure exploited by conventional methods, and many existing near-field formulations remain only gridless by discretizing range and angle and thus inheriting mismatch, coherence, and resolution loss. This paper develops a continuous 2D super-resolution framework for hybrid near-field measurements that avoids range and angle gridding. The key idea is to reparameterize distance through inverse range, which reveals a compact spectral structure for the near-field spherical-wave manifold. Building on this observation, we introduce a panelized weighted fitting strategy that converts the range-dependent Fresnel terms into a stable transform-domain representation, resulting in a lifted mode, in which each continuous range-angle pair is embedded as a structured rank-one atom and the measurement model remains linear under hybrid combining. Recovery is then posed as a 2D atomic norm minimization, with path localization certified through a dual polynomial over the transformed domain. Numerical experiments show exact support recovery in the noiseless setting using only few compressed hybrid measurements. These results establish the proposed inverse-range atomic norm viewpoint as a new gridless foundation for near-field sensing and channel estimation in hybrid XL-MIMO and integrated sensing and communication systems.

items.title: Generic Local Identifiability Does Not Imply Generic Global Identifiability in Linear Networks
items.summary: We give a counterexample to the implication from generic local to generic global identifiability for linear networks with a fixed topology, independently unknown edge coefficients, and selected excited and measured nodes. A six-node network with nine unknown coefficients has exactly two compatible parameter vectors generically. Adding six excited and measured nodes preserves this ambiguity while making the added coefficients directly recoverable. The resulting twelve-node structure has forty-two independent unknown coefficients and zero diagonal. For every positive bound on the largest eigenvalue magnitude, a nonempty open set of parameters has two distinct compatible networks satisfying that bound. This holds for both real and complex coefficients. Other open regions have exactly one admissible solution. The proof uses a rational transformation exchanging the two solutions and a common limiting matrix whose fourth power vanishes. Exact rational-number certificates verify an explicit pair. The construction also extends algebraically when the unknown coordinates are whole rational transfer functions. Genericity in prescribed numerator and denominator coefficient families, and the requirement that every transfer function vanish at infinite frequency, remain separate questions.

items.title: Link Both Views: Cross-Image Routing Attention for Dual-Endpoint V2I Beam-Pair Power Prediction
items.summary: For sensing-aided communications, single-endpoint sensing offers only a partial view of propagation, motivating link-centric sensing across both endpoints. We propose cross-image routing attention (CIRA) for sparse association and mutual enhancement of propagation-relevant features from dual-endpoint RGB images. Building on CIRA, CiFormer predicts millimeter-wave (mmWave) beam-pair power matrices for vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I) communications. Experiments show that CiFormer reduces mean absolute error and improves top-1 beam-pair selection accuracy by 3.15 percentage points over the strongest baseline. Visualizations and ablation studies support dual-endpoint sensing and selective cross-view interaction in capturing propagation-relevant dependencies, suggesting broader applications in wireless tasks beyond beam prediction.

items.title: Estimating Closed-Loop Multiple-Input Single-Output Dynamic Systems using Gaussian Processes
items.summary: This paper extends complex Gaussian process regression-based transfer function (TF) estimation from the single-input single-output setting to closed-loop multiple-input single-output (MISO) systems. Accurate estimation of individual TFs in closed-loop MISO systems is challenging as feedback and correlation between measured signals can obscure the contributions of each input. We formulate a Gaussian process-based estimator for MISO systems, provide analytical conditions under which each system module can be separately identified, and show that the estimator converges to the true TFs in the zero noise limit. Moreover, we demonstrate how conventional closed-loop bias handling techniques relying on external excitation can be employed to construct appropriate regressors. Monte Carlo simulations support the analytical identifiability results and highlight the trade-off between closed-loop bias and error introduced by constructing exogenous regressors partly from endogenous signals. The presented work offers an expressive, nonparametric alternative to existing estimation approaches for MISO systems, while providing a probabilistic characterization of the estimation uncertainty.

items.title: Amplitude-Dependent Bode Diagrams via Scaled Relative Graphs
items.summary: Scaled Relative Graphs (SRGs) provide an intuitive graphical frequency-domain method for the analysis of Nonlinear (NL) systems, generalizing the Nyquist diagram. In this paper, we develop a method for computing $L_2$-gain bounds for Lur'e systems over bounded frequency and amplitude ranges. We do this by restricting the input space of the SRG both in frequency and energy content, and using methods from Sobolev theory. The resulting gain bounds over restricted sets of inputs are less conservative than bounds computed over the entire $L_2$, and yield three-dimensional NL generalization of the Bode diagram, plotting $L_2$-gain as function of both input frequency and energy content. In the zero-energy limit, the Linear Time-Invariant (LTI) Bode diagram is recovered, and at the infinite-energy zero-frequency limit, we recover the $L_2$-gain. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated on an example that resembles Phase-Locked Loop dynamics.

items.title: Revisiting Error Feedback for Model Quantization
items.summary: We study causal error-feedback coefficients as design variables for model quantization. Modeling instantaneous quantization errors as independent, zero-mean variables with a common fixed variance, we formulated a metric-dependent trace problem for designing feedback coefficients. The formulation resembles fixed-order GPTQ/LDLQ feedback and supports Jacobian-aware designs that account for downstream error propagation. For a positive-definite metric $\boldsymbol{H}$, we prove that the joint rotation-feedback trace minimum is $n\det(\boldsymbol{H})^{1/n}$ and present an attaining pair using the geometric mean decomposition. Experiments on synthetic networks, trained MLPs, and language models show benefits from downstream-sensitive feedback, but also reveal that trace optimality need not improve finite-level performance. Small QAT experiments further illustrate direct loss-driven feedback tuning with fixed or trainable network weights.

items.title: Preliminary Exploration of Large Models Based on Self-Supervised Learning for Health Monitoring of Power Electronic Converters
items.summary: Current artificial intelligence (AI) methods for power electronics converters make limited use of the abundant unlabeled data generated during real-world operation. This underexplored resource holds significant potential for advancing model performance. To address this gap, this paper presents PE-TSFM, a time-series foundation model tailored for power module health monitoring. The model adopts the PatchTST architecture combined with self-supervised learning and is trained on more than 143 million timestamps, where over 98\% of this training data is unlabeled and collected directly from an operating traction converter. In degradation classification tasks, PE-TSFM achieves an accuracy of 87\%, considerably surpassing five conventional time-series AI models whose performance ranges from 27\% to 45\%. These results demonstrate the model's strong few-shot learning capability and generalization across different operating conditions. This work promotes a shift from narrowly focused models in power electronics toward unified, scalable foundation models that can unlock value from large-scale unlabeled operational data.

items.title: Self-Supervised Source-Filter Model of Speech Production
items.summary: Deep learning models of speech seldom represent the source-filter process by which speech is produced, relying instead on latent features with no physical correspondence to articulation or phonation. We propose SoFilNet, a self-supervised, differentiable Source-Filter Network that estimates the parameters of speech production directly from the raw waveform: a source, specified by fundamental frequency (F0), voicing and the aperiodicity of five frequency bands, and a filter, specified by ordered formant poles, additional poles that shape the rest of the spectral envelope, and antiresonance zeros. The model is trained only to reconstruct the input speech; no formant or pitch annotation is used. Since per-bin spectral losses favor blurred spectra wherever the model is uncertain, we train F0 and voicing against autocorrelation pseudo-labels refined with the model's own filter, aperiodicity against the periodic fraction of each band, and formant sharpness against spectral contrast. On VTR-FORMANTS, the estimated formants attain the lowest mean error among the reported methods, including supervised trackers, and on the unseen PTDB-TUG corpus the F0 frame error matches the best classical tracker and is lower than that of all learned trackers. The parameters are also consistent with speech production theory: aperiodicity rises with frequency and orders phone classes by the turbulence of their excitation, and the zeros deepen on nasal consonants, the lower one rising with place of articulation.

items.title: Network Reconstruction in Consensus Algorithms with Hidden Agents
items.summary: Reconstructing the parameters that encode the influence between model variables based on time-series measurements represents an outstanding question in the theory of complex network-coupled systems. Here, we propose a solution to this problem for a class of noisy leader-follower consensus algorithms, where one has access to measurements only from the followers but not from the leaders. Leveraging the directed Laplacian coupling of such systems, we present an autoregressive expansion of the observed dynamics which can be truncated at different orders, depending on the memory of the leaders. When their memory is short, this allows one to correctly reconstruct the full dynamical matrix with hidden leader agents, provided some additional assumption on the system to lift the degeneracy in the reconstruction. We illustrate and check the theory using numerical simulations for the cases of both a single and multiple hidden leaders.

items.title: Panoramic Out-of-Distribution Segmentation
items.summary: Panoramic imaging enables capturing 360° images with an ultra-wide Field-of-View (FoV) for dense omnidirectional perception, which is critical to applications such as autonomous driving and augmented reality. However, current panoramic semantic segmentation methods fail to identify outliers, and pinhole out-of-distribution segmentation (pinhole-OoS) models perform unsatisfactorily in the panoramic domain due to pixel distortions and background clutter. To address these issues, we introduce a new task, Panoramic Out-of-Distribution Segmentation (PanOoS), with the aim of achieving comprehensive and safe scene understanding. Furthermore, we propose the first solution, POS, which adapts to the characteristics of panoramic images through text-guided prompt distribution learning. Specifically, POS integrates a disentanglement strategy designed to materialize the cross-domain generalization capability of CLIP. The proposed Prompt-based Restoration Attention (PRA) optimizes semantic decoding by prompt guidance and self-adaptive correction, while Bilevel Prompt Distribution Learning (BPDL) refines the manifold of per-pixel mask embeddings via semantic prototype supervision. Besides, to compensate for the scarcity of PanOoS datasets, we establish two benchmarks: DenseOoS, which features diverse outliers in complex environments, and QuadOoS, captured by a quadruped robot with a panoramic annular lens system. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of POS, with AuPRC increasing and FPR95 decreasing by 34.25 and 21.42 percentage points, respectively, compared with RbA on DenseOoS, outperforming state-of-the-art pinhole-OoS methods. Moreover, POS achieves leading closed-set segmentation capabilities and advances the development of panoramic understanding. Code and datasets will be available at https://github.com/MengfeiD/PanOoS.

items.title: Forecasting Brain Tracer Distribution from Pre-Contrast MRI: A Comparison of Direct Regression and Flow Matching
items.summary: Intrathecal contrast-enhanced MRI shows how a tracer injected into the cerebrospinal fluid spreads through the brain, but requires repeated scans over 24--48\,h. We therefore ask how much of the later tracer distribution can be predicted from the pre-contrast scan and elapsed time alone. Using 104 training patients (878 MRI volumes), we compared a direct image-to-image regression model with a more complex generative model based on conditional flow matching, and tested both on 23 held-out patients and on 51 patients from a separate cohort with idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (INPH). The direct model reduced the error of simply copying the pre-contrast scan by about 60\% in held-out patients and 25\% in the INPH cohort, and its predicted change maps agreed with the observed tracer enhancement rather than only reproducing anatomy. The generative model was less accurate in both cohorts. A substantial part of the later tracer distribution is therefore predictable from the patient's brain anatomy as seen on pre-contrast MRI, and the added model complexity gave no benefit at this data scale. With prospective validation, such forecasts could be studied for patient stratification and treatment planning in intrathecal therapies.

items.title: LiDAL-Assisted RLNC-NOMA in OWC Systems
items.summary: Optical wireless communication (OWC) is a key enabler for immersive indoor data transmission in future wireless networks. However, managing multi-user interference remains challenging in dense indoor OWC deployments with multiple optical access points (APs) serving multiple users. In this paper, we propose a dual-function OWC system for communication and localization. For data transmission, we design non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) combined with random linear network coding (RLNC): NOMA serves multiple users simultaneously via power-domain multiplexing, while RLNC improves decoding robustness under residual noise and processing impairments. The system is assisted by a light detection and localization (LiDAL) module that estimates users' spatio-temporal presence and location to enable dynamic user association. LiDAL also supports channel state information (CSI) estimation in realistic indoor scenarios where CSI may be noisy and/or highly correlated. We evaluate RLNC-NOMA by analyzing the probability of successful decoding and comparing it with conventional NOMA and orthogonal schemes. In addition, we derive the Cramer-Rao lower bound (CRLB) to evaluate the localization accuracy. The results indicate that RLNC-NOMA increases the probability of successful decoding, and that the proposed unbiased location estimator achieves 44% better CSI accuracy than the baseline CSI estimation and improves the overall system performance.

items.title: Lifted Restricted Isometry Property and Fast Algorithm for Spectral Compressed Sensing With Near-Optimal Sample Complexity
items.summary: This paper studies the spectral compressed sensing problem, which aims to recover an $r$-spectrally-sparse signal of length $N$ from linear compressive measurements. We reformulate the problem as the recovery of a low-rank Hankel matrix. Motivated by this formulation, we propose a Lifted Restricted Isometry Property (LRIP) for the measurement matrix and show that Gaussian measurement matrices satisfy LRIP under certain conditions. Unlike classical RIP, LRIP imposes a rank constraint in the lifted matrix domain while taking measurements in the signal domain through the adjoint Hankel operator. To solve the resulting nonconvex problem efficiently, we introduce a Fast Iterative Hard Thresholding (FIHT) algorithm. Based on LRIP, we show that FIHT converges linearly to the true signal with high probability using $\mathcal{O}(r \ln r \ln^2 N)$ scaled Gaussian measurements, which is near-optimal up to log factors and improves the state-of-the-art order of $r^2$ for nonconvex Hankel methods. Extensive numerical results demonstrate the superiority of FIHT as compared to state-of-the-art convex methods in terms of phase transitions, computational time, and robustness to noise.

items.title: MagNav: A Dual-Core Magnetic Track Guidance Framework for Lighting-Invariant Navigation in Two-Wheeled Robots
items.summary: Two-Wheeled Inverted Pendulum (TWIP) robots are useful for studying how to control systems that are naturally unstable and have fewer actuators than degrees of freedom. Adding autonomous line-following to these robots is challenging because steering and balancing are closely linked. Most existing systems use infrared sensors, which can be affected by changes in lighting, such as sunlight or shadows, making them reliable only indoors. This paper presents a self-balancing robot that can follow a line using a magnetic track guidance system. By using a five-channel analog Hall-effect sensor array, the robot is not affected by optical interference. The control system uses a cascaded PID structure: the inner loop keeps the robot balanced using data from an inertial measurement unit with a complementary filter, while the outer loop adjusts steering based on the magnetic sensor readings. Stepper motors provide precise torque control without needing extra rotary encoders. For comparison, an optical sensor module was also included. Tests show that the magnetic guidance system keeps accurate tracking even in very bright lighting, over 10,000 Lux, while the optical system loses accuracy and sometimes fails. This design provides a reliable, lighting-independent solution for autonomous navigation in places like factories, warehouses, and outdoor paths.

items.title: A Foundation Model for Large-Scale Wireless Network Planning , Operation and Optimization
items.summary: Wireless cellular networks form the connective tissue of human society, sustained by a continuous physical dialogue between engineered infrastructure and its surroundings. Radio signals emitted from base stations traverse terrain, diffract around buildings and scatter through streets before reaching billions of users. Together, these interactions produce the city-wide radio environment on which every network decision rests. Shaping this environment through deployment and optimization determines the connectivity societies rely on, yet learning it effectively at city scale and generalizing across diverse cities and deployments remain open challenges. Here we answer positively by introducing ChaRT, a foundation model that learns transferable radio representations from measurement reports generated by deployed cellular networks. These reports provide abundant multi-cell, multi-beam observations without dedicated campaigns, forming a scalable data foundation for city-scale learning. ChaRT embeds beam-level angular structure, network hierarchy and propagation-regime diversity in its architecture, and is pretrained through context-aware masked beam modelling and self-distillation with channel-model-constrained augmentation. We pretrain ChaRT on over one billion reports comprising 18.2 billion beam-level observations from 3,503 cells in one city. With a single set of weights, ChaRT reconstructs radio environments in unseen cities and transfers to radio map construction, new-site prediction and network parameter tuning. With only 1% of labelled data, it supports user localization, beam prediction, propagation scenario classification and estimation of the signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio. The learned representation further enables beamspace clustering for reusable radio-grid construction. These results establish ChaRT as a transferable foundation for network-wide intelligence.

items.title: Hidden Commitment Power Is Powerless
items.summary: A principal who offers a contract may renege when her default option is sufficiently attractive. The size of this temptation, which inversely measures her commitment power, is often the principal's private information. This paper asks how contracting outcomes change under this information asymmetry. Disciplining off-path beliefs with the Intuitive Criterion, I find that every type of principal behaves and earns payoffs as if she were commonly known to have the least commitment power. Hidden commitment power is therefore powerless, although commitment power can be valuable under symmetric information. The result delivers an unambiguous policy lesson on how to mitigate this information asymmetry prior to contracting: only measures that improve the worst case have value. In an application to credit rating, when the cost of a rating system grows with its number of grades, a rating system that sorts issuers into ordered bands is optimal, and each issuer contracts on the terms warranted by the floor of her band.

items.title: Multiple-Player War of Attrition with Asymmetric Private Values
items.summary: This paper studies a war of attrition over public good provision among multiple ex-ante asymmetric privately informed players. In equilibrium, asymmetry leads to a stratified behavior pattern in which at most one player provides the public good at time zero with a positive probability, while the other players can become active one after another, each at a player-specific activation time, before which even his highest type does not provide the good. The equilibrium is essentially unique: the types who never provide make the players' costs of providing a saddle point of the equilibrium dynamics. Comparing two players in the same war, I show that the one with lower cost, more impatience, or a value distribution tilted toward high values in the sense of a higher revelation rate provides earlier at every value, other things equal. In large societies, the cost of delay is determined by the highest value across players.

items.title: Locally Robust Inference with Outcomes Predicted by Machine Learning
items.summary: Many parameters of interest in economics depend on outcomes generated by machine learning (ML).These generated outcomes are subsequently used in standard econometric estimation and typically treated as observed, a practice that threatens the validity of downstream inference. Empirically relevant cases include dynamic treatment effects under sequential exogeneity, long-term effects with surrogates, the partially linear model with an ML-predicted outcome, productivity persistence with an unrestricted production function and constructed instruments, and outcomes residualized of confounding variation. This paper develops a three-step locally robust GMM framework for valid inference when the dependent variable is generated by ML. We construct a debiased moment condition that augments the identifying moment with first- and second-step influence functions, making inference on the parameter of interest locally insensitive to regularization and model selection biases at both steps. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the proposed estimator and illustrate its finite-sample performance through Monte Carlo simulations. We also apply the method to U.S. mortgage data to study conditional Black--White disparities in a race-blind ML default-risk score. The score predicts subsequent default well overall, but the conditional disparity embedded in the score is much smaller than the corresponding disparity in realized serious delinquency; accounting for first-step estimation also raises the naive out-of-sample estimate of the score disparity.

items.title: Equitable Auctions
items.summary: We study how auction design shapes surplus division among bidders. We introduce a parsimonious ex post equity notion and examine standard multi-unit auctions. The equity-optimal pricing depends sharply on the private-common value composition. Among mixed-price auctions, at one extreme, uniform pricing is always optimal for pure common values and, at the other, pay-as-bid pricing is preferred for pure private values under standard regularity assumptions. For any fixed monotone allocation rule, we characterize a BNIC interim-IR implementation that equalizes surplus ex post across all bidders and is revenue-maximizing among those that equalize surplus ex ante; efficient allocation permits parity among winners.

items.title: Estimating treatment-effect heterogeneity across sites, in multi-site randomized experiments with few units per site
items.summary: Multi-site randomized experiments, which are common in economics and medicine, can reveal how treatment effects vary across settings. However, differences between site-specific estimates reflect both treatment-effect heterogeneity and estimation noise. We build on established measurement-error corrections and develop new ones to study this heterogeneity in experiments with many sites and few units per site. In particular, our results can be used to estimate the variance and centered third moment of treatment effects across sites, relate site effects to untreated outcomes, conduct mediation analyses, assess the roles of provider effectiveness and site responsiveness, and study heterogeneity in local average treatment effects (LATEs) under imperfect compliance. We apply our methods to counseling programs delivered by public and private providers in about 200 French employment offices. Average employment gains of about 2 percentage points conceal cross-site standard deviations of intention-to-treat effects of 8 to 9 percentage points. We also find substantial LATE heterogeneity.Effects are negatively associated with untreated employment rates. The two programs also tend to be more effective in the same sites, consistent with a role for heterogeneous site responsiveness.

items.title: A Structural Matrix Autoregression Framework for International Spillovers
items.summary: Understanding how macroeconomic shocks propagate across countries requires structural models that can jointly identify country-specific shocks and their international transmission. Yet extending structural vector autoregressions (SVARs) to large multi-country systems is challenging due to rapidly increasing dimensionality, computational costs, and the proliferation of identifying restrictions. This paper develops a Bayesian Structural Matrix Autoregression (BSMAR) framework that exploits the natural matrix structure of international macroeconomic data. By separating dependence across economic variables from dependence across countries, the framework provides a parsimonious representation that substantially reduces the dimensionality of large structural systems. We develop a Bayesian sampling algorithm for posterior inference that accommodates zero, sign, and ranking (magnitude) restrictions, allowing established SVAR identification schemes to be combined with a novel approach to identifying contemporaneous international spillovers. Applying the model to quarterly data for 15 economies, we find substantial heterogeneity in international shock transmission, with demand shocks playing a more prominent role than supply shocks in generating cross-country spillovers.

items.title: Allocative Efficiency and the Returns to Innovation
items.summary: Innovation changes welfare through the technology it adds and the reallocation it causes between producers with different markups. When producers set markups, an innovator's own output and price adjustments have no private value at the margin, so reallocation reaches its profit only through others' responses. For an innovator small in its markets, none of the change in allocative efficiency, which is of the same order as its cost saving, reaches its profit under quantity or price competition. A process innovator is paid its cost saving, forgoing its own and downstream markups on added output. For U.S. public firms in 2015, these average 14 to 26 percent of that saving, and allocative efficiency rises or falls by more than a tenth of the private return for innovators holding 56 percent of sales. With estimated spillovers, patenting firms' R&D has a social return 6.24 times its private return.

items.title: Contracting under Misspecification
items.summary: This paper studies agency problems when both parties worry that the model linking action to output is misspecified. With observable actions, an optimal contract is linear in output, so performance pay arises solely to share misspecification exposure, the slope reflects the parties' relative robustness concerns, and its allocation is Pareto efficient. With hidden actions, this sharing rule survives and incentives add a nonlinear correction. Misspecification concerns can polarize effort by making intermediate actions impossible to implement. Moreover, ambiguity across competing models has asymmetric effects: uncertainty about desired actions raises the principal's payoff, whereas uncertainty about deviations can lower it.

items.title: Identification and Inference for Algorithmic Frontiers with Selective Labels
items.summary: This paper provides identification results to characterize a fairness-accuracy (FA) frontier, and statistical inference tools to test hypotheses and build a confidence set for the FA-frontier, when outcomes are observed only for selected individuals. When the selection process is unrestricted but loss is measured in specific ways, we provide a characterization of the sharp identification region of the FA-frontier. When the observed distribution rules out frontier membership for a binary status quo algorithm, we construct a single alternative algorithm that improves both groups' accuracy without worsening fairness, uniformly over all admissible distributions of missing labels. For any loss functions, under selection on observables and strict overlap assumptions, we obtain point identification and propose a debiased machine learning estimator, derive its asymptotic distribution, and show how this can be used to carry out inference for the FA-frontier.

items.title: A unified decision model for Bayesian ambiguity and non-affine statistics
items.summary: This paper studies decision functionals under ambiguity when pure-risk evaluation is determined by a general, possibly non-affine statistic. We represent ambiguity perception by a Bayesian second-order model over first-order models and encode ambiguity attitude with a separate parameter. We formulate four consistency and monotonicity properties for decision functionals combining these objects. We show that second-order averaging does not generally preserve these properties for non-affine statistics, including expected shortfall, the industry-standard risk measure. To address this limitation, we introduce an ambiguity iron, a mapping from a second-order model and an ambiguity attitude to an ambiguity set of first-order models. Worst-case evaluation over this set preserves the chosen statistic as the pure-risk criterion. We construct an ambiguity iron by distorting the second-order model and show that it produces convex and compact sets of predictive models. We derive formulas for several classes of statistics and, in parametric settings, a sample-based approximation for the distorted expectation. Portfolio examples illustrate how ambiguity perception and attitude affect evaluations and allocations. Under posterior concentration and continuity of the parametrization, the ambiguity sets contract, and the associated decision functionals converge to their pure-risk values. We also describe a KL-based robustification for possible model misspecification.

items.title: Metric geometry for ranking-based voting: Tools for learning electoral structure
items.summary: In this paper, we develop the metric geometry of ranking statistics, proving that the two major permutation distances in the statistics literature -- Kendall tau and Spearman footrule -- extend naturally to incomplete rankings with both coordinate embeddings and graph realizations. This gives us a unifying framework that allows us to connect popular topics in computational social choice: metric preferences (and metric distortion), polarization, and proportionality. As an important application, the metric structure enables efficient identification of blocs of voters and slates of their preferred candidates. Since the definitions work for partial ballots, we can execute the methods not only on synthetic elections, but on a suite of real-world elections. This gives us robust clustering methods that often produce an identical grouping of voters -- even though one family of methods is based on a Condorcet-consistent ranking rule while the other is not.

items.title: Testing Tail-Index Homogeneity via Exceedance-Covariate Independence
items.summary: We propose a test of whether the tail index of a heavy-tailed outcome is homogeneous across observed covariates. The key observation is that, under tail-index homogeneity, normalized log exceedances are asymptotically independent of the covariates even when tail frequencies vary with them. This leads to a simple-to-implement permutation test based on distance covariance, without estimating conditional tail indices or specifying the form of tail-index heterogeneity. For the global and locally balanced versions, we establish validity for order-statistic thresholds and give conditions for consistency and local power. Local balancing selects extremes within two covariate groups and can improve power when tail selection concentrates the covariates. Simulations illustrate these gains. In French motor insurance data, upper conditional quantiles vary with risk characteristics, but the tail-index tests do not reject a common tail index.

items.title: Generative AI Availability, Grades, and Student Satisfaction at a Large University
items.summary: The availability of generative AI (GenAI) has raised concerns that college students substitute GenAI for cognitive effort, earning high grades without learning. If this "GenAI substitution hypothesis" is true, grades should rise disproportionately in GenAI-susceptible courses--those relying more on assessments like take-home problem sets and essays rather than in-class exams. Student satisfaction (self-reported understanding and interest) may also shift. We test this hypothesis using syllabus and administrative data from a large U.S. university (2016-2025; 138,386 students; 72,730 course offerings). We measure GenAI susceptibility by extracting assessment types from syllabi with a human-validated LLM pipeline. We then use a difference-in-differences design comparing courses before and after ChatGPT's release, modeling COVID-19 effects as persistent or transient. Effects on grades and satisfaction are small and sensitive to COVID modeling choices, with no detectable differences by students' prior academic preparation. Exploratory analyses show that the link between pre-college test scores and grades has not detectably weakened in more susceptible courses, and that instructors have been making courses less susceptible since before ChatGPT. Our findings temper concerns that GenAI inflates grades and reduces satisfaction, partly because instructors may adapt their pedagogy.

items.title: Revealing Structured Heterogeneity
items.summary: In this paper, we study models of restricted heterogeneity. While the random utility model allows for arbitrary heterogeneity among rational types, we consider the case when an analyst ex-ante restricts the set of rational types to some smaller set of allowable types. We study the behavioral content, the model fit, and the identification properties of restrictions of this form. We find that all three of these can be connected through a common value function that is constructed from observable data. Consistency with a model of restricted heterogeneity is characterized by this value function achieving a value of one, while model fit is given by a value that is potentially less than one. The partially identified set for a given model of restricted heterogeneity is characterized by way of the subdifferential of this value function.

items.title: Quality at Stale Prices
items.summary: We study a continuous-time game in which a firm privately chooses quality and a public-information pricing desk revises its posted price at Poisson opportunities. Customers learn from purchases and silence. For an open set of primitives, we construct an equilibrium in which a previously optimal price sustains quality even though the desk would lower it upon revision. Quality costs exceed every immediate sales return, making the continuation reward necessary. We characterise both the resulting quality episodes and their lifetime incidence. A purchase ends an episode by raising reputation, a revision by changing the price, and silence by lowering reputation. Near the zero-quality threshold, the quality probability has a limiting parabolic profile and most episodes end through silence. If $δ$ is the cost shortfall below that threshold, the expected lifetime number of high-quality decisions and the probability of any such decision are both of order $δ^{3/2}$ from a specified upstream state. The persistent type is eventually learned, strategic quality ceases, and prices settle at type-specific levels. The construction is local at fixed finite discounting.

items.title: Heterogeneous Policy Effects in Comparative Case Studies with Treated-Unit Microdata
items.summary: This article develops an identification framework for heterogeneous policy effects when individual-level data are available only in the treated jurisdiction. The framework combines outcome changes from repeated cross-sections within that jurisdiction with a population-average effect identified from aggregate panel data. Under conditional relative parallel trends and overlap, this information identifies subgroup effects standardized to the treated jurisdiction's overall post-treatment covariate distribution, but generally not effects averaged over each subgroup's own distribution. I establish how these subgroup-average effects can nevertheless be recovered using covariate-specific aggregate effects or additional pretreatment observations under assumptions about the evolution of untreated trends. Simulations and an application to the Massachusetts health reform illustrate the framework.

items.title: Persuading an inattentive and privately informed receiver
items.summary: This paper studies the persuasion of a receiver who accesses information only if she exerts costly attention effort. A sender designs an experiment to persuade the receiver to take a specific action. The experiment affects the receiver's attention effort, that is, the probability that she updates her beliefs. Persuasion has two margins: an extensive margin (effort) and an intensive margin (action). The receiver's utility exhibits a complementarity property in information and effort. By leveraging this property, we establish an equivalence between experiments and persuasion mechanisms à la Kolotilin et al.~(2017). In applications, the sender's optimal strategy involves censoring favorable states.

items.title: Auction-based allocation of routes in capacity-constrained networks
items.summary: We study the route-set allocation problem between end nodes in capacity-constrained flow networks with transfer costs. We introduce an origin--destination (OD) bidding language, in which a participant bids for bounded conic combinations of inlet--outlet--quantity licences and the mechanism performs the routing through a network-flow optimising winner-determination problem. We then study payment rules for the OD mechanism. Under a restricted model with openly and uniformly priced sources and bidders who are indifferent to the source of the gas, the Vickrey--Clarke--Groves (VCG) payment is core-stable; the key structural fact is that in this regime some optimal aggregate flows never use a physical pipe in both directions, so the winner-determination problem reduces to a single-commodity network flow whose value is submodular in the set of active bidders. If source access is allowed to depend on the individual consumer -- a realistic feature, e.g. when gas deals are embedded in bilateral political bargaining -- the reduction fails and VCG payments may lie strictly outside the core. For this general model we propose a dual (nodal) pricing rule derived from the shadow prices of the flow-conservation constraints, and prove it is always core-stable, at the cost of dominant-strategy incentive compatibility. Illustrative examples accompany each result.

items.title: Random sets from the perspective of metric statistics
items.summary: Since the seminal work by Beresteanu and Molinari(2008), the random set theory and related inference methods have been widely applied in partially identified econometric models. Meanwhile, there is an emerging field in statistics for studying random objects in metric spaces, called metric statistics. This paper clarifies a relationship between two fundamental concepts in these literatures, the Aumann and Fréchet means, and presents some applications of metric statistics to econometric problems involving random sets.

items.title: Ideological Bias in LLMs' Economic Causal Reasoning
items.summary: Do large language models (LLMs) exhibit systematic ideological bias when reasoning about economic causal effects? As LLMs are increasingly used in policy analysis and economic reporting, where directionally correct causal judgments are essential, this question has direct practical stakes. We present a systematic evaluation by extending the EconCausal benchmark with ideology-contested cases - instances where intervention-oriented (pro-government) and market-oriented (pro-market) perspectives predict divergent causal signs. From 10,490 causal triplets (treatment-outcome pairs with empirically verified effect directions) derived from top-tier economics and finance journals, we identify 1,056 ideology-contested instances and evaluate 20 state-of-the-art LLMs on their ability to predict empirically supported causal directions. We find that ideology-contested items are consistently harder than non-contested ones, and that across 17 of 20 models, accuracy is systematically higher when the empirically verified causal sign aligns with intervention-oriented expectations than with market-oriented ones. Moreover, when models err, their incorrect predictions disproportionately lean intervention-oriented, and this directional skew is not eliminated by one-shot in-context prompting. These results highlight that LLMs are not only less accurate on ideologically contested economic questions, but systematically less reliable in one ideological direction than the other, underscoring the need for direction-aware evaluation in high-stakes economic and policy settings.

items.title: Which Text Matters: Handling Model Uncertainty in Text-as-Data Regressions, with an Application to Central Bank Communication
items.summary: Social scientists routinely convert text into covariates like topic shares, ideal points or sentiment scores, and insert them into statistical models of interest. This two-step design is convenient, but it is rarely guided by theory: little tells the analyst which text-based covariates to construct or include. Each approach embodies contestable measurement choices, and competing operationalizations of the same construct can support different conclusions, so a single research question gives rise to a menu of competing regression models. Which text constructed covariates belong in a model, and in what functional form, is thus a problem of model uncertainty. We propose spike-and-slab generalized additive models (SSGAMs), which jointly select covariates and determine whether their effects are linear or nonlinear. We illustrate the approach with the communication of a powerful unelected institution, asking which of 45 competing text indicators from 224 monthly European Central Bank press conferences, spanning late 2002 to mid-2025, track professional inflation expectations. A sparse set is selected; widely used alternatives, and every tested nonlinear effect, carry no incremental information.

items.title: Coalition-Proof Disclosure
items.summary: We study generalized verifiable disclosure by a sender with type-independent preferences. We first characterize all perfect Bayesian equilibria as partitions of the sender's types into coalitions ordered by payoff. An equilibrium survives our coalition-proofness criterion if no group of types can profitably coordinate an announced deviation that only they are able and willing to join. Coalition-proof equilibria are greedy partitions: at each step, a coalition of the remaining types attains the highest payoff consistent with equilibrium. In our general setting, coalition-proof equilibria may fail to exist. We establish existence under restrictions on preferences and evidence: quasiconcavity with message completeness, betweenness, cheap talk with message completeness, and payoff degradation. For a disclosure game with maximally rich evidence, we show that the sender's ex-ante payoff in a coalition-proof equilibrium is a piecewise linear tent over the belief simplex, analogous to the concave closure in Bayesian persuasion and the quasiconcave closure in cheap talk.

items.title: Building a Sovereign Benchmark The Limits of Private Coordination
items.summary: Public debt supplies liquidity and collateral services only if institutions coordinate on using the same claim. We study this coordination when use carries a recurring cost and a benefit that rises with other users. Above a quality threshold, two positive-adoption equilibria exist, and under best responses the initial user base decides between collapse and high adoption. Under logit choice, as the population grows and noise vanishes, the long-run distribution selects high adoption only above a strictly higher threshold. Debt issuance improves market depth but eventually dilutes backing per claim. This trade-off creates a range of debt levels supporting the liquidity premium of public debt in macroeconomic models and a narrower range supporting its long-run selection. At the boundary of the wider range, the premium is discontinuous. A matching transfer that corrects the adoption externality makes stationary selection maximize network surplus. Transfers can also help launch a network without permanent support.

items.title: Rewarding Noise: Incentives in Decentralized A/B Testing
items.summary: Many firms that run A/B tests struggle with low statistical power, increasing the risk that launch decisions are driven by noise rather than true impact. We argue that in decentralized organizations, low power can reflect misaligned incentives: product teams choose what and how to test on a customer-facing experience to maximize their private reward, while the experience owner sets evaluation rules and launch criteria to optimize the experience. We formalize this interaction via a principal-agent model and show that evaluating tests using raw impact estimates creates a reward to sampling noise. Correctly calibrated posterior-mean evaluation removes this reward and creates a local incentive to reallocate toward fewer, more precise tests of more ambitious ideas. Using data on A/B tests run at Amazon, we document patterns consistent with these model predictions. After an Amazon experience shifted to posterior-mean-based evaluation in 2024, test volume declined while both precision and the dispersion of true impacts increased, more than doubling signal-to-noise ratios. Our results highlight that A/B testing methodologies can shape not only measurement and launch decisions, but which tests are pursued in the first place.

items.title: Who Keeps a Bubble Alive? Skin in the Game and the Survival of Rational Bubbles
items.summary: We study how retained ownership supports the value of an asset that pays no dividends and is held only for resale. A sponsor chooses hidden maintenance that determines market survival, bears its full cost, and captures only the benefit accruing to its retained tokens. A positive stationary equilibrium exists if and only if retention meets an endogenous minimum. Under additional curvature restrictions, retention above this threshold supports two positive stationary equilibria. Conditional on survival, prices below the upper equilibrium converge to the lower one while the upper price is the largest feasible initial valuation. Greater retention expands the feasible price interval. Credible news that future retention will be below the minimum causes an immediate collapse through backward unraveling. The model identifies a governance channel through which insider unlocks can affect valuation without changing total token supply or fundamental cash flows.

items.title: Does Rank Still Matter? Position Bias When AI Agents Shop on Our Behalf
items.summary: When shopping is delegated to AI agents, it is unclear whether the ranking advantage documented for humans persists. Across 7,000 sessions with five large language models (LLMs) and varying reasoning effort, we compare AI agents with human field data. AI agents search more extensively than human consumers. As with humans, lower-ranked listings are less likely to be inspected, although the effect is smaller for AI agents. Unlike humans, AI agents show a pattern consistent with the lost-in-the-middle effect, whereby middle listings have the lowest probability of inspection. At the choice stage, position effects are concentrated at lower reasoning effort, but higher effort reduces the middle penalty for every LLM that exhibits it. These findings suggest that, when search is delegated, displayed attributes may matter more than placement, and that exposure to position bias depends on how the AI agent is configured.

items.title: Whom Do AI Agents Work For? Role Assignment Induces Sponsorship Bias in LLM Recommenders
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) now serve as conversational shopping assistants on platforms that also sell advertising. These AI agents face a conflict of duty. They advise consumers who rely on their judgment, yet are deployed by platforms that benefit when sponsored listings are chosen. Sponsorship disclosures, designed to allow consumers to penalize paid placements, now reach the AI agent rather than the consumer, and the agent's evaluation of them is hidden from the consumer. Drawing on the fiduciary concept of conflict of duty, we argue that an agent's evaluation of a sponsored listing should not depend on which party deployed it. In controlled choice experiments, we manipulate assigned roles in the system prompt to name either a traveler or a booking platform as the agent's principal. Platform delegation significantly attenuates the penalty that agents apply to sponsored listings and weakens the skepticism that disclosure triggers in their reasoning traces. We replicate out findings across LLMs and reasoning depths. A second study decomposes the disclosure label and shows that the divergence between the two delegates widens significantly when the paid placement is attributed to the platform. Stricter terminology ("Sponsored" instead of "Promoted") lowers choice of paid listings but does not close this gap when the platform is named. The findings show that disclosure mandates designed for human consumers cannot by themselves protect consumers in AI-mediated commerce.

items.title: Shopping by algorithm: How agentic AI deploys human heuristics as a surrogate consumer
items.summary: Consumers increasingly delegate purchasing decisions to Large Language Models (LLMs) acting as surrogate consumers. Using "Tool-Lab," an adaptation of information-board process tracing that places product attributes behind costly tool calls, we examine how marketing pricing cues (i.e., just-below pricing and promotional framing) influence AI shopping agents. Across eight commercially deployed LLMs from three providers, we trace pre-choice information acquisition. Under zero cost, pricing cues rarely mislead. Imposing acquisition costs under a vague goal prompt leads LLMs to omit diagnostic attributes required to compute unit price and choose suboptimal choices resembling human heuristics. Relative to a specific goal prompt that mainly preserves diagnostic search and choice optimality, a vague goal prompt under constraints creates a search-mediated vulnerability. This research demonstrates that marketing heuristics in delegated AI shopping are governed by storefront information architecture, not necessarily immutable LLM flaws.

items.title: Congestion Games with Heterogeneous Valuations: An Optimal Transport Approach
items.summary: In emerging urban mobility and logistics applications, such as advanced air mobility, electric vehicle charging, and shared service systems, agents with heterogeneous valuations choose among multiple outcomes while sharing congested resources. Existing congestion game and resource-allocation models, however, typically restrict either the structure of heterogeneous outcome preferences or the form of congestion externalities. We introduce a nonatomic congestion game framework in which agents have multidimensional heterogeneous valuations over a finite set of outcomes, with the population represented by a measure over the valuation space. We show that, although there is a continuum of heterogeneous agents, both Nash equilibria and social optima admit finite-dimensional characterizations. Nash equilibria are characterized by aggregate flows and outcome-level threshold vectors, while social optima admit a semi-discrete optimal transport formulation characterized by aggregate flows and strategy-level Kantorovich dual potentials. For separable utilities and latency functions $\ell_e$ such that $x\mapsto x\ell_e(x)$ is convex for every resource $e$, the social welfare problem becomes a convex optimization problem, and we characterize social optima through marginal congestion costs and capacity-dual prices. Our results provide a geometric characterization of congestion games with multidimensional heterogeneous valuations and connect nonatomic congestion games with semi-discrete optimal transport.

items.title: Improving and Balancing Task Allocation with Market Design
items.summary: In balanced task allocation, a firm allocates stochastically arriving tasks to workers. Balance requires that workers complete the same number of tasks or have equally difficult task allocations. Prominently, U.S. foster care agencies rotate allocation across workers to satisfy balance. The Rotation mechanism is highly inefficient and could contribute to poorer welfare and productivity for workers. I take a market design approach to construct the Dynamic Pseudomarket Mechanism (DPM). It satisfies the institutional balance constraint, Pareto efficiency, and approximate incentive compatibility. I develop a data-driven bound on DPM's expected productivity because DPM could increase or decrease productivity in practice. Simulation results indicate this approach can accurately predict DPM's effects with minimal data. The theoretical results underpinning the bound establish that, in large random markets, workers' welfare converges to the maximum in fractional, multi-unit Pareto efficient matchings, a finding of independent interest.

items.title: COWPEA (Candidates Optimally Weighted in Proportional Election using Approval voting)
items.summary: This paper describes COWPEA (Candidates Optimally Weighted in Proportional Election using Approval voting), a method of proportional representation that uses approval voting. It has also been used in other contexts and been referred to as Random Priority, though it is underdeveloped in the literature. COWPEA optimally elects an unlimited number of candidates with potentially different weights to a body, rather than giving a fixed number equal weight. A non-deterministic Approval-Based Committee (ABC) version that elects a fixed a number of candidates with equal weight is known as COWPEA Lottery. This is the only proportional ABC method known to pass the criteria of monotonicity, strong candidate Pareto efficiency, multi-winner participation, Independence of Irrelevant Ballots (IIB), Independence of Universally Approved Candidates (IUAC), Independence of Irrelevant Alternatives (IIA) and independence of clones. It is also possible to convert COWPEA and COWPEA Lottery to use score ballots. They are compared against Optimal PAV and Optimal PAV Lottery, which have good overall criterion compliance but fail monotonicity. This paper introduces Perfect Representation In the Limit (PRIL) as a new proportionality criterion.

items.title: You've Got to be Efficient: Ambiguity, Misspecification and Variational Preferences
items.summary: This article introduces a framework for evaluating statistical decisions under both prior ambiguity and likelihood misspecification.
